      "title": "Weight Magnitude Variance Regularization Tests Whether Superposition Capacity Drives Subject-Disjoint Generalization",
      "summary": "This experiment tests whether explicitly encouraging high variance in attention query weight row magnitudes improves generalization to held-out subjects by enhancing representational superposition capacity. Building on Superposition Yields Robust Neural Scaling [5], which identifies geometric overlaps between representation vectors as a driver of neural scaling, this study directly manipulates superposition capacity through weight magnitude distribution rather than weight decay.",
      "research_question": "Does increasing the variance of weight magnitudes in attention query projections improve subject-disjoint generalization by enabling more efficient feature superposition?",
      "hypothesis": "Adding a loss term that maximizes variance of query projection weight row norms will improve held-out classification accuracy on subject-disjoint data compared to standard training without this regularization.",
      "keywords": ["superposition", "weight regularization", "subject-disjoint generalization", "transformer", "feature capacity"],
      "rationale": "Paper [5] establishes that strong superposition enables neural scaling through geometric overlaps between representation vectors, controlled via weight decay.       "area": "Deep Learning Theory / Representation Learning",
      "open_problem": "What mechanisms control representational superposition capacity during training, and does superposition capacity causally affect out-of-distribution generalization to new subjects?",

            "1. At each training step during loss_term phase, retrieve target weight tensor W with shape [64, 64]",

          "invariants": ["regularization_loss is differentiable w.r.t. W", "comparator lambda=0 produces baseline behavior", "identical seeds ensure paired comparison validity", "no gradient clipping or modification beyond autograd"]

        "target_power": 0.9,

        "mechanistic_rationale": "Paper [5] shows superposition (representing more features than dimensions via geometric overlaps) enables neural scaling. related_work.title: Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness
related_work.abstract: Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.04805 proportion (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort confirmed this degradation with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Negative controls involving entropy minimization and fixed noise performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over explicit entropy maximization for robustness tasks in this regime.

related_work.title: Generalization Aware Minimization
related_work.abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) algorithms have effectively improved neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions of the training loss landscape, which tend to generalize poorly. However, the underlying mechanisms of SAM are not fully understood, and recent studies question whether its bias toward flatter regions is why it improves generalization. In this work, we introduce Generalization-Aware Minimization (GAM), a generalized version of SAM that employs multiple perturbation steps instead of SAM's single-step perturbations. This allows GAM to directly guide model parameters toward areas of the landscape that generalize better. We show that the expected true (test) loss landscape is a rescaled version of the observed training loss landscape and demonstrate how GAM's multiple perturbative updates can be designed to optimize this expected true loss. Finally, we present a practical online algorithm that adapts GAM's perturbative steps during training to improve generalization, and we empirically validate its superior performance over SAM on benchmark datasets. We believe GAM sheds light on the generalization improvements of sharpness-based algorithms and can inspire the development of optimizers with even better generalization.

related_work.title: Generalization Bound and Learning Methods for Data-Driven Projections in Linear Programming
related_work.abstract:
How to solve high-dimensional linear programs (LPs) efficiently is a fundamental question.
Recently, there has been a surge of interest in reducing LP sizes using *random projections*, which can accelerate solving LPs independently of improving LP solvers. 
This paper explores a new direction of *data-driven projections*, which use projection matrices learned from data instead of random projection matrices.
Given training data of $n$-dimensional LPs, we learn an $n\times k$ projection matrix with $n > k$. 
When addressing a future LP instance, we reduce its dimensionality from $n$ to $k$ via the learned projection matrix, solve the resulting LP to obtain a $k$-dimensional solution, and apply the learned matrix to it to recover an $n$-dimensional solution.

On the theoretical side, a natural question is: how much data is sufficient to ensure the quality of recovered solutions? We address this question based on the framework of *data-driven algorithm design*, which connects the amount of data sufficient for establishing generalization bounds to the *pseudo-dimension* of performance metrics. We obtain an $\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(nk^2)$ upper bound on the pseudo-dimension, where $\tilde{\mathrm{O}}$ compresses logarithmic factors. We also provide an $\Omega(nk)$ lower bound, implying our result is tight up to an $\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(k)$ factor. 

On the practical side, we explore two simple methods for learning projection matrices: PCA- and gradient-based methods. While the former is relatively efficient, the latter can sometimes achieve better solution quality. Experiments demonstrate that learning projection matrices from data is indeed beneficial: it leads to significantly higher solution quality than the existing random projection while greatly reducing the time for solving LPs.

related_work.title: Generalization Bound of Gradient Flow through Training Trajectory and Data-dependent Kernel
related_work.abstract: Gradient-based optimization methods have shown remarkable empirical success, yet their theoretical generalization properties remain only partially understood. In this paper, we establish a generalization bound for gradient flow that aligns with the classical Rademacher complexity bounds for kernel methods—specifically those based on the RKHS norm and kernel trace—through a data-dependent kernel called the loss path kernel (LPK). Unlike static kernels such as NTK, the LPK captures the entire training trajectory, adapting to both data and optimization dynamics, leading to tighter and more informative generalization guarantees. Moreover, the bound highlights how the norm of the training loss gradients along the optimization trajectory influences the final generalization performance. The key technical ingredients in our proof combine stability analysis of gradient flow with uniform convergence via Rademacher complexity. Our bound recovers existing kernel regression bounds for overparameterized neural networks and shows the feature learning capability of neural networks compared to kernel methods. Numerical experiments on real-world datasets validate that our bounds correlate well with the true generalization gap.

related_work.title: Low-Entropy Latent Variables Hurt Out-of-Distribution Performance
related_work.abstract: We study the relationship between the entropy of intermediate representations and a model's robustness to distributional shift. We train models consisting of two feed-forward networks end-to-end separated by a discrete $n$-bit channel on an unsupervised contrastive learning task. Different masking strategies are applied after training that remove a proportion of low-entropy bits, high-entropy bits, or randomly selected bits, and the effects on performance are compared to the baseline accuracy with no mask. We hypothesize that the entropy of a bit serves as a guide to its usefulness out-of-distribution (OOD). Through experiment on three OOD datasets we demonstrate that the removal of low-entropy bits can notably benefit OOD performance. Conversely, we find that top-entropy masking disproportionately harms performance both in-distribution (InD) and OOD.

related_work.title: Regularization and Optimal Multiclass Learning
related_work.abstract: The quintessential learning algorithm of empirical risk minimization (ERM) is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning. Relatedly, the practice of machine learning is rife with considerably richer algorithmic techniques, perhaps the most notable of which is regularization. Nevertheless, no such technique or principle has broken away from the pack to characterize optimal learning in these more general settings. The purpose of this work is to precisely characterize the role of regularization in perhaps the simplest setting for which ERM fails: multiclass learning with arbitrary label sets. Using one-inclusion graphs (OIGs), we exhibit optimal learning algorithms that dovetail with tried-and-true algorithmic principles: Occam’s Razor as embodied by structural risk minimization (SRM), the principle of maximum entropy, and Bayesian inference. We also extract from OIGs a combinatorial sequence we term the Hall complexity, which is the first to characterize a problem’s transductive error rate exactly. Lastly, we introduce a generalization of OIGs and the transductive learning setting to the agnostic case, where we show that optimal orientations of Hamming graphs – judged using nodes’ outdegrees minus a system of node-dependent credits – characterize optimal learners exactly. We demonstrate that an agnostic version of the Hall complexity again characterizes error rates exactly, and exhibit an optimal learner using maximum entropy programs.

related_work.title: Generalization Analysis for Multi-Label Learning
related_work.abstract: Despite great advances in algorithms for multi-label learning, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization is still in the early stage. Some recent theoretical results has investigated the generalization performance of multi-label learning under several evaluation metrics, however, how to reduce the dependency on the number of labels, explicitly introduce label correlations, and quantitatively analyze the impact of various inductive biases in the generalization analysis of multi-label learning is still a crucial and open problem. In an attempt to make up for the gap in the generalization theory of multi-label learning, we develop several novel vector-contraction inequalities, which exploit the Lipschitz continuity of loss functions, and derive generalization bounds with a weaker dependency on the number of labels than the state of the art in the case of decoupling the relationship among different components, which serves as theoretical guarantees for the generalization of multi-label learning. In addition, we derive the generalization bound for Macro-Averaged AUC and analyze its relationship with class-imbalance. The mild bounds without strong assumptions explain the good generalization ability of multi-label learning with first-order label correlations and high-order label correlations induced by norm regularizers.

related_work.title: Minimization of the Training Makespan in Hybrid Federated Split Learning
related_work.abstract: Parallel Split Learning (SL) allows resource-constrained devices that cannot participate in Federated Learning (FL) to train deep neural networks (NNs) by splitting the NN model into parts. In particular, such devices (clients) may offload the processing task of the largest model part to a computationally powerful helper, and multiple helpers may be employed and work in parallel. In hybrid federated and split learning (HFSL), on the other hand, devices can participate in the training process through any of the two protocols (SL and FL), depending on the system's characteristics. This could considerably reduce the maximum training time over all clients (makespan), especially in highly heterogeneous scenarios. In this paper, we study the joint problem of the training protocol selection, client-helper assignments, and scheduling decisions, to minimize the training makespan. We prove this problem is NP-hard and propose two solution methods: one based on the decomposition of the problem by leveraging its inherent symmetry, and a second fully scalable one. Through numerical evaluations using our testbed's measurements, we build a solution strategy comprising these methods. Moreover, this strategy finds a near-optimal solution and achieves a shorter makespan than the baseline schemes by up to 71%.

related_work.title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey
related_work.abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Furthermore, we highlight key application scenarios, emphasizing their real-world impact. Finally, we identify persistent challenges and propose future research directions. A detailed summary of the methods reviewed for the generalization of OOD in time series can be accessed at https://tsood-generalization.com.

related_work.title: Generalization Bounds for Autoregressive Processes and In-Context Learning
related_work.abstract: In this paper, we derive generalization results for next-token risk minimization in autoregressive processes of unbounded order. Our starting point is to relate the empirical loss to the denoising loss, which requires no additional assumptions compared to fixed-order Markovian models. We then show that, under a mixing or rephrasability condition on the data-generating process and assuming a stable hypothesis class, the out-of-sample generalization error concentrates around the denoising error. These results characterize sample complexity in terms of the number of tokens, rather than the number of i.i.d. sequences. As a primary application, we interpret in-context learning as a special case of autoregressive prediction and derive sample complexity bounds under similar conditions. Importantly, the properties of individual in-context tasks determine the generalization rates, without requiring assumptions on mixture processes. This perspective suggests that in-context learning can exploit the task decomposition to learn efficiently.

related_work.title: Length Generalization via Auxiliary Tasks
related_work.abstract:
_Length generalization_, the ability of sequence models to
  generalize to sequences longer than those encountered during
  training, remains a key challenge for transformers,
  especially in tasks requiring algorithmic reasoning. Existing
  theoretical understanding of length generalization is limited, often providing
  only asymptotic results or focusing on specific problem classes or
  architectural variants, while empirical approaches frequently rely on
  ad hoc and often fragile techniques.

  In this work we introduce a novel framework for analyzing and
  proving length generalization bounds under specified, verifiable assumptions. A key
  outcome of the theory is the identification of a natural set of
  _auxiliary_ tasks, intricately related to the primary task structure,
  such that strong performance on these auxiliary tasks, alongside the
  primary task, provably guarantees length generalization within the framework.  This
  motivates a multi-task training procedure that explicitly optimizes
  performance on both the primary and the identified auxiliary tasks.

  Empirical evaluations on a variety of synthetic benchmarks
  known to be challenging for length generalization, including sequence
  sorting, and reversal, demonstrate that our proposed method yields
  significant improvements in generalization to substantially longer
  sequences.

related_work.title: Regularization by Denoising via Fixed-Point Projection (RED-PRO)
related_work.abstract: Inverse problems in image processing are typically cast as optimization tasks, consisting of data-fidelity and stabilizing regularization terms. A recent regularization strategy of great interest utilizes the power of denoising engines. Two such methods are the Plug-and-Play Prior (PnP) and Regularization by Denoising (RED). While both have shown state-of-the-art results in various recovery tasks, their theoretical justification is incomplete. In this paper, we aim to bridge between RED and PnP, enriching the understanding of both frameworks. Towards that end, we reformulate RED as a convex optimization problem utilizing a projection (RED-PRO) onto the fixed-point set of demicontractive denoisers. We offer a simple iterative solution to this problem, by which we show that PnP proximal gradient method is a special case of RED-PRO, while providing guarantees for the convergence of both frameworks to globally optimal solutions. In addition, we present relaxations of RED-PRO that allow for handling denoisers with limited fixed-point sets. Finally, we demonstrate RED-PRO for the tasks of image deblurring and super-resolution, showing improved results with respect to the original RED framework.

related_work.title: A Watermark for Low-entropy and Unbiased Generation in Large Language Models
related_work.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have highlighted the risk of misusing them, raising the need for accurate detection of LLM-generated content. In response, a viable solution is to inject imperceptible identifiers into LLMs, known as watermarks. Previous work demonstrates that unbiased watermarks ensure unforgeability and preserve text quality by maintaining the expectation of the LLM output probability distribution. However, previous unbiased watermarking methods suffer from one or more of the following issues: (1) requiring access to white-box LLMs during detection, (2) incurring long detection time, (3) being not robust against simple watermarking attacks, (4) failing to provide statistical guarantees for the type II error of watermark detection, and (5) being not statistically unbiased for low-entropy scenarios, which hinder their deployment in practice. This study proposes the Sampling One Then Accepting (STA-1) method, a watermark that can address all of these issues. Moreover, we discuss the tradeoff between watermark strength and text quality for unbiased watermarks. We show that in low-entropy scenarios, unbiased watermarks face a tradeoff between watermark strength and the risk of unsatisfactory outputs. Experimental results on both low-entropy and high-entropy datasets demonstrate that STA-1 achieves text quality and watermark strength comparable to existing unbiased watermarks, with a low risk of unsatisfactory outputs. Implementation codes for this study are available online (hidden for peer review).

related_work.title: Singular Bayesian Neural Networks
related_work.abstract:
Bayesian neural networks promise calibrated uncertainty but require $O(mn)$ parameters for standard mean-field Gaussian posteriors. We argue this cost is often unnecessary, particularly when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay.
By parameterizing weights as $W = AB^{\top}$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$, 
$B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$, we induce a posterior that is \emph{singular} 
with respect to the Lebesgue measure, concentrating on the rank-$r$ manifold. This 
singularity captures structured weight correlations through shared latent 
factors, geometrically distinct from mean-field's independence assumption. We derive PAC-Bayes generalization bounds whose complexity term scales as $\sqrt{r(m+n)}$ instead of $\sqrt{m n}$, and prove loss bounds that decompose the error into optimization and rank-induced bias using the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem. We further adapt recent Gaussian complexity bounds for low-rank deterministic networks to Bayesian predictive means. 
Empirically, across MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers on standard benchmarks, our method achieves competitive predictive performance while using up to $33\times$ fewer parameters than 5-member Deep Ensembles. It substantially improves OOD detection and often improves calibration relative to mean-field and perturbation baselines, while Deep Ensembles can still be stronger on in-distribution likelihood-based metrics.

related_work.title: Minimization I.I.D. Prophet Inequality via Extreme Value Theory: A Unified Approach
related_work.abstract: The I.I.D. Prophet Inequality is a fundamental problem where, given $n$ independent random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ drawn from a known distribution $\mathcal{D}$, one has to decide at every step $i$ whether to stop and accept $X_i$ or discard it forever and continue. The goal is to maximize or minimize the selected value and compete against the all-knowing prophet. For maximization, a tight constant-competitive guarantee of $\approx 0.745$ is well-known (Correa et al, 2019), whereas minimization is qualitatively different: the optimal constant is distribution-dependent and can be arbitrarily large (Livanos and Mehta, 2024). In this paper, we provide a novel framework via the lens of Extreme Value Theory to analyze optimal threshold algorithms. We show that the competitive ratio for the minimization setting has a closed form described by a function $\Lambda$, which depends only on the extreme value index $\gamma$; in particular, it corresponds to $\Lambda(\gamma)$ for $\gamma \leq 0$. Despite the contrast of maximization and minimization, our framework turns out to be universal and we recover the results of (Kennedy and Kertz, 1991) for maximization as well. Surprisingly, the optimal competitive ratio for maximization is given by the same function $\Lambda(\gamma)$, but for $\gamma \geq 0$. Along the way, we obtain several results on the algorithm and the prophet's objectives from the perspective of extreme value theory, which might be of independent interest. We next study single-threshold algorithms for minimization. Using extreme value theory, we generalize the results of (Livanos and Mehta, 2024) which hold only for special classes of distributions, and obtain poly-logarithmic in $n$ guarantees. Finally, we consider the $k$-multi-unit prophet inequality for minimization and show that there exist constant-competitive single-threshold algorithms when $k \geq \log{n}$.

related_work.title: Low-Entropy Watermark Detection via Bayes' Rule Derived Detector
related_work.abstract: Text watermarking, which modify tokens to embed watermark, has proven effective in detecting machine-generated texts. Yet its application to low-entropy texts like code and mathematics presents significant challenges. A fair number of tokens in these texts are hardly modifiable without changing the intended meaning, causing statistical measures to falsely indicate the absence of a watermark. Existing research addresses this issue by rely mainly on a limited number of high-entropy tokens, which are considered flexible for modification, and accurately reflecting watermarks. However, their detection accuracy remains suboptimal, as they neglect strong watermark evidences embedded in low entropy tokens modified through watermarking. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Bayes’ Rule derived Watermark Detector (BRWD), which exploit watermark information from every token, by leveraging the posterior probability of watermark’s presence. We theoretically prove the optimality of our method in terms of detection accuracy, and demonstrate its superiority across various datasets, models, and watermark injection strategies. Notably, our method achieves up to 50% and 70% relative improvements in detection accuracy over the best baselines in code generation and math problem-solving tasks, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/cczslp/BRWD.

related_work.title: Regularization Shortcomings for Continual Learning
related_work.abstract: In most machine learning algorithms, training data is assumed to be independent and identically distributed (iid). When it is not the case, the algorithm's performances are challenged, leading to the famous phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting. Algorithms dealing with it are gathered in the Continual Learning research field. In this paper, we study the regularization based approaches to continual learning and show that those approaches can not learn to discriminate classes from different tasks in an elemental continual benchmark: the class-incremental scenario. We make theoretical reasoning to prove this shortcoming and illustrate it with examples and experiments. Moreover, we show that it can have some important consequences on continual multi-tasks reinforcement learning or in pre-trained models used for continual learning. We believe that highlighting and understanding the shortcomings of regularization strategies will help us to use them more efficiently.

related_work.title: IMSE: Intrinsic Mixture of Spectral Experts Fine-tuning for Test-Time Adaptation
related_work.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has been widely explored to prevent performance degradation when test data differ from the training distribution. However, fully leveraging the rich representations of large pretrained models with minimal parameter updates remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose Intrinsic Mixture of Spectral Experts (IMSE) that leverages the spectral experts inherently embedded in Vision Transformers. We decompose each linear layer via singular value decomposition (SVD) and adapt only the singular values, while keeping the singular vectors fixed. We further identify a key limitation of entropy minimization in TTA: it often induces feature collapse, causing the model to rely on domain-specific features rather than class-discriminative features. To address this, we propose a diversity maximization loss based on expert-input alignment, which encourages diverse utilization of spectral experts during adaptation. In the continual test-time adaptation (CTTA) scenario, beyond preserving pretrained knowledge, it is crucial to retain and reuse knowledge from previously observed domains. We introduce Domain-Aware Spectral Code Retrieval, which estimates input distributions to detect domain shifts, and retrieves adapted singular values for rapid adaptation. Consequently, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on various distribution-shift benchmarks under the TTA setting. In CTTA and Gradual CTTA, it further improves accuracy by 3.4 percentage points (pp) and 2.4 pp, respectively, while requiring 385 times fewer trainable parameters. Our code is available at https://github.com/baek85/IMSE.

related_work.title: SLOWED: Slow Tuning and Low-Entropy Masking for Safe Chain-of-Thought Distillation
related_work.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation improves the reasoning capabilities of Small Language Models (SLMs) by fine-tuning on high-quality rationales generated by large language models, but such fine-tuning degrades their safety alignment. Existing safety alignment methods require extra computation or annotated safety data absent from standard distillation pipelines. We propose **SLOWED** (Slow Tuning and LOW-Entropy Masking Distillation), a safe CoT distillation framework that addresses safety degradation without additional data or computational overhead. SLOWED integrates two complementary strategies: Slow Tuning constrains weight updates to a neighborhood of the initial model after each epoch, preserving its pre-trained safety representations; Low-Entropy Masking excludes low-entropy tokens from the distillation loss, concentrating gradients on high-entropy reasoning tokens where learning is most beneficial. Experiments on three SLMs demonstrate that SLOWED achieves a safety ratio of 56.38\% on Qwen2.5-1.5B, 2.4$\times$ higher than the strongest distillation baseline, while simultaneously attaining the highest out-of-distribution reasoning accuracy of 57.10\%. Ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of both modules: Slow Tuning sustains safety in early training stages, while Low-Entropy Masking extends safe fine-tuning to later epochs. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SLOWED-BAE9.

related_work.title: Regularization for Uplift Regression
related_work.abstract: We address the problem of regularization of linear regression models in uplift modeling and heterogeneous treatment effect estimation. We consider interaction models which are commonly used by statisticians in medicine and social sciences to estimate the causal effect of a treatment, and introduce a new type of such a model. We demonstrate the equivalence of all interaction models when no regularization is present, and that this is no longer the case when the model is regularized. Interaction terms introduce implicit correlations between treatment and control coefficients into the regularizer, a fact which has not been previously noted. The correlations depend on the type of interaction model, and by interpreting the regularizer as a prior distribution we were able to pinpoint cases when a given regularized interaction model is most appropriate. An interesting property of the proposed new interaction type is that it allows for smooth interpolation between two types of uplift regression models: the double model and the transformed target model. Our results are valid for both ridge (\(L_2\)) and Lasso (\(L_1\)) regularization. Experiments on synthetic data fully confirm our analyses. We also compare the usefulness of various regularization schemes on real data.

related_work.title: Mean-State Entropy Hierarchies and Classical Communication through Quantum Convolutions
related_work.abstract: Quantum convolution provides a discrete-variable analogue of classical convolution, with the mean state capturing the stabilizer structure preserved under repeated convolution. We establish a finite-step entropy hierarchy generated by compatible stabilizer dephasings. Along every compatible isotropic flag, the entropy increases toward the mean-state entropy ceiling, while the relative-entropy distance to the mean state decomposes exactly into successive coherence losses and a terminal classical nonuniformity. Optimizing over compatible subspaces yields an intrinsic entropy profile of the state. For quantum convolutional channels, Weyl covariance reduces the one-shot classical communication problem to minimal output entropy. A spectral-transfer argument shows that suitable stabilizer inputs reproduce stabilizer-measurement distributions of the environment as channel-output spectra. This gives a computable Holevo lower bound over all complete stabilizer measurements; its compatible restriction is characterized by the entropy hierarchy and refines the previous mean-state bound of Bu, Gu, and Jaffe. The bound is exact for stabilizer-diagonal environments, for which the Holevo capacity is strongly additive, and yields a single-letter formula for a nonstabilizer qutrit family. The same family also exhibits a coexistence region with simultaneously positive classical and quantum communication rates

related_work.title: Transformer Copilot: Learning from The Mistake Log in LLM Fine-tuning
related_work.abstract: Large language models are typically adapted to downstream tasks through supervised fine-tuning on domain-specific data. While standard fine-tuning focuses on minimizing generation loss to optimize model parameters, we take a deeper step by retaining and leveraging the model’s own learning signals, analogous to how human learners reflect on past mistakes to improve future performance. We first introduce the concept of Mistake Log to systematically track the model’s learning behavior and recurring errors throughout fine-tuning. Treating the original transformer-based model as the Pilot, we correspondingly design a Copilot model to refine the Pilot’s inference performance via logits rectification. We name the overall Pilot-Copilot framework the Transformer Copilot, which introduces (i) a novel Copilot model design, (ii) a joint training paradigm where the Copilot continuously learns from the evolving Mistake Log alongside the Pilot, and (iii) a fused inference paradigm where the Copilot rectifies the Pilot’s logits for enhanced generation. We provide both theoretical and empirical analyses on our new learning framework. Experiments on 12 benchmarks spanning commonsense, arithmetic, and recommendation tasks demonstrate that Transformer Copilot consistently improves performance by up to 34.5%, while introducing marginal computational overhead to Pilot models and exhibiting strong scalability and transferability. Our code is released at https://github.com/jiaruzouu/TransformerCopilot.

related_work.title: Minimization of Task Completion Time in Wireless Powered Mobile Edge-Cloud Computing Networks
related_work.abstract: To enable resource-constrained wireless devices (WDs) to process the computation-intensive and latency-sensitive computation tasks, the wireless powered mobile edge computing (WP-MEC) network has been proposed as a promising approach. Incorporating mobile cloud computing (CC) in the WP-MEC network, we investigate the wireless powered mobile edge-CC (WP-MECC) network, where the WDs first harvest energy from a hybrid access point (HAP), and then consume the harvested energy to compute the tasks locally, offload them to the HAP for computation, or offload them to the cloud server (CS) via the relaying of the HAP. To pursue fairness among the WDs, we minimize the maximum task completion time (TCT) of WDs by jointly optimizing the time resources, computing mode selection, and computation resources. We prove the minimization problem is NP-hard. To tackle the problem, we decompose it into the subproblem and top problem, and propose an alternate optimization-based resource allocation and the computing mode selection (ARACM) algorithm with low computational complexity, which achieves a comparable performance with the exhaustive search method in terms of the minimal maximum TCT of WDs. Moreover, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based resource allocation and the computing mode selection (DRACM) algorithm with less execution latency than the ARACM algorithm. Numerical results show that the two proposed algorithms achieve satisfactory performance in terms of the minimal maximum TCT of WDs and execution latency.

related_work.title: Generalization and Learnability in Multiple Instance Regression
related_work.abstract:
Multiple instance regression (MIR) was introduced by Ray and Page (2001) as an analogue of multiple instance learning (MIL) in which we are given bags of feature-vectors (instances) and for each bag there is a bag-label which matches the label of one (unknown) primary instance from that bag. The goal is to compute a hypothesis regressor consistent with the underlying instance-labels. A natural approach  is to find the best primary instance assignment and regressor optimizing the mse loss on the bags though no formal generalization guarantees were known. Our work is the first to prove generalization error bounds for MIR when the bags are drawn i.i.d. at random. Essentially, with high probability any MIR regressor with low error on sampled bags also has low error on the underlying instance-label distribution.

We next study the complexity of linear regression on MIR bags, shown to be NP-hard in general by Ray and Page (2001), who however left open the possibility of arbitrarily good approximations. Significantly strengthening previous work, we prove a strong inapproximability bound: even if there exists zero bag-loss MIR linear regressor on a collection of $2$-sized bags with labels in $[-1,1]$, it is NP-hard to find an MIR linear regressor with bag-loss  $< C$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$.

Our work also proposes a model training method for MIR based on a novel weighted assignment loss, geared towards handling overlapping bags which have not received much attention previously.  We conduct empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets showing that our method outperforms the baseline MIR methods.

related_work.title: Learning a Cost-Effective Strategy on Incomplete Medical Data
related_work.abstract: Deep learning techniques have shown remarkable success in classification tasks. However, the prerequisite for high accuracy is that data is easily accessible, which is unrealistic since most features come at a cost. Under a medical scenario, each feature is associated with a medical test that costs a certain amount of money. And doctors would ask patients to do consecutive tests until they are confident enough to make a final diagnosis, whereas the overall cost incurred during the process is often ignored. In this paper, we propose to learn a cost-effective strategy which at the same time hastens the decision process. As is often the case where both medical records and initial feature values of a new patient are incomplete, we design a framework consisting of two components, the oracle classifier and the feature selector, to tackle the challenges. The classifier incorporates a sequence encoder that can handle any set of feature values in various sizes. And the selector efficiently learns the cost-effective strategy based on the state-of-art reinforcement learning techniques. Experimental results have shown that under the same classification accuracy, our strategy is superior to other related approaches in terms of the overall cost.

Additionally, *Generalization Bound and Learning Methods for Data-Driven Projections in Linear Programming* explores data-driven projections, which relates to input projection strategies used to reduce dimensionality.

Deep learning models for temporal data often operate in regimes where distribution shifts and non-stationary dynamics challenge out-of-distribution generalization. While architectural advances such as Transformers have improved representation capacity, the mechanistic role of weight spectra in facilitating feature learning versus kernel regime behavior remains poorly understood. Standard regularization techniques, such as weight decay, penalize parameter magnitude but do not explicitly constrain the geometry of the weight matrix singular values. This omission is significant in finite-width networks, where the distribution of singular values can dictate whether the model operates in a rich feature learning regime or collapses toward a kernel-like limit. Clarifying this relationship is critical for designing regularization strategies that enhance robustness in resource-constrained edge AI, where subject-disjoint generalization is paramount.

Current literature offers conflicting perspectives on the role of entropy and structure in weight matrices. Some work suggests that low-rank structures or singular value decay can reduce parameter costs while maintaining performance, implying that concentrating energy into dominant modes might be beneficial. Conversely, other research indicates that low-entropy representations can hurt out-of-distribution performance, suggesting that diversity in representations or weights may be necessary for robustness. Despite these theoretical insights, there is no direct investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. This gap leaves practitioners without empirical guidance on whether spectral shaping is a viable alternative to standard weight decay for temporal tasks.

This paper presents a preregistered experiment testing the hypothesis that enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning compared to standard weight decay. We utilize a calibrated testbed with a Transformer encoder on inertial signal data, employing an official subject-disjoint split to ensure robust evaluation. - We formulate and test a preregistered hypothesis regarding spectral entropy minimization in input projections for temporal feature learning.

**Generalization in Sequential Data**

Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments, which pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. Deriving generalization results for autoregressive processes requires relating empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than independent sequences [10]. Length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers with limited existing theoretical understanding, often requiring auxiliary tasks to guarantee performance on longer sequences [11]. Despite advances in algorithms, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization in multi-label learning is still in the early stage, with open problems regarding label dependencies [7]. This operator is the right expression of the hypothesis because it directly penalizes spectral dispersion without constraining the magnitude of the weights, which is handled by the baseline weight decay. By isolating the spectral geometry, the method tests whether the distribution of singular values independently contributes to generalization in temporal tasks. The comparator, standard weight decay, neutralizes magnitude effects but allows the singular value spectrum to evolve freely based on gradient dynamics. The hypothesis predicts that the intervention will yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. The operator is designed to induce a feature learning regime where the model relies on a subset of dominant temporal modes, potentially improving robustness to subject-specific noise in the input signal. The method does not alter the architecture or optimization algorithm beyond the addition of the spectral entropy term, ensuring that any observed differences are attributable to the spectral constraint.

The method relies on the assumption that the SVD computation is stable across seeds and that the entropy term is differentiable enough to guide optimization effectively.

The experiment utilizes the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with raw inertial signals, employing the official subject-disjoint split to ensure robust evaluation. This design choice tests what the research question asks by preventing information leakage between training and testing subjects, which a random split would have hidden. Subject-disjoint splits are critical for assessing generalization to unseen users, a key requirement for edge AI deployment. A random split would inflate accuracy estimates by allowing the model to memorize subject-specific signatures rather than learning generalizable temporal features.

We employed 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds to ensure statistical power and reproducibility. This number of seeds allows for precise estimation of the confidence intervals around the mean contrast, reducing the risk of false positives due to random initialization variance. Pairing every condition on one seed buys a direct comparison of the intervention and baseline under identical initialization noise, costs being the computational overhead of running multiple conditions per seed. This pairing reduces variance in the contrast estimate, making it easier to detect small but meaningful effects.

The analysis includes two negative controls to rule out indistinguishable outcomes. The first negative control establishes the performance of the standard weight decay baseline, while the second ensures that implementation details of the regularization term do not drive results. The results refute the prediction that the intervention would yield higher accuracy exceeding the margin. The data indicates that spectral entropy minimization does not enhance feature learning in this setting compared to standard weight decay.

=== discussion ===
The quantitative findings indicate that minimizing spectral entropy of input projections does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. This result contrasts with the hypothesis that concentrating energy into dominant temporal modes would facilitate feature learning. In the primary cohort, the contrast was 0.0004419, and in the replication cohort, it was 0.002549, both far below the preregistered margin of 0.0125098. The confidence intervals included zero in both cases, leading to an inconclusive decision regarding superiority. This null finding clarifies the mechanistic role of weight spectra, suggesting that spectral shaping alone is insufficient for robustness in this regime.

Relating these findings to prior work, the results align with evidence that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures [1]. While that study refuted entropy maximization, this study refutes entropy minimization for spectral geometry, suggesting that explicit entropy constraints on weights may not be the correct lever for generalization in transformers. The findings also contrast with work suggesting that low-entropy latent variables hurt out-of-distribution performance, where removing low-entropy bits benefited robustness [5]. Here, enforcing low entropy on weights did not help, implying that weight spectral entropy and latent representation entropy may play different roles in generalization.

The results extend understanding of singular value decay in Bayesian networks, where low-rank parameterization captured structured weight correlations [14]. While that work found parameter efficiency benefits, this study found no accuracy benefit from spectral entropy minimization in a deterministic setting. This suggests that the benefits of low-rank structures may be primarily computational or specific to Bayesian posterior approximations rather than deterministic regularization. The findings do not support the idea that steering weights toward low-entropy spectra improves generalization aware minimization outcomes [2]. Instead, standard weight decay appears sufficient for this task, aligning with observations that empirical risk minimization failures require specific regularization principles not met by spectral entropy alone [6].

The replication cohort confirmed the primary result, strengthening the conclusion that the effect is null rather than a statistical anomaly. The consistency across 86 seeds suggests that the lack of improvement is robust to initialization variance. This outcome guides regularization design for resource-constrained edge AI, indicating that practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over spectral entropy minimization for robustness tasks. The results do not contradict the general challenge of distribution shifts in time series [9], but they specify that spectral entropy minimization is not the solution to this challenge in input projections. Future work should investigate whether spectral constraints on attention matrices rather than input projections yield different outcomes.

=== limitations ===
This study has several limitations. First, the experiment is limited to a single dataset and architecture, specifically the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset and a Transformer encoder. While the subject-disjoint split ensures robust evaluation, the findings may not generalize to other temporal domains such as speech or financial time series. Second, the spectral entropy term was applied only to the input projection weights. It is possible that applying the constraint to attention matrices or feed-forward layers could yield different results, but this was outside the scope of the preregistered hypothesis. Third, the study used a fixed worthwhile margin based on prior power analysis, but the true effect size might be smaller than detectable even with 43 seeds per cohort. Finally, the computational overhead of SVD calculations at each step may limit scalability to larger models, though this did not affect the accuracy results. These limitations suggest that while the null result is robust for this setting, broader claims require further investigation.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks. The results did not support the preregistered hypothesis, with both primary and replication cohorts showing inconclusive differences below the worthwhile margin. The proposed condition did not yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline. For someone choosing between these methods, the findings indicate that standard weight decay is sufficient and spectral entropy minimization offers no accuracy benefit. To settle the question next, future work should investigate spectral constraints on other model components or in different architectural regimes.

=== discussion ===
The quantitative findings indicate that minimizing spectral entropy of input projections does not enhance subject-disjoint generalization in temporal transformers. Instead, the data suggests that standard weight decay is sufficient for this task, and additional spectral constraints provide no benefit. This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset and a specific Transformer architecture. This study found that enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights does not improve held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay. Deep learning models deployed in edge AI environments frequently encounter distribution shifts that degrade performance, particularly in temporal domains where non-stationary dynamics are prevalent. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset exemplifies this challenge, requiring models to generalize across subjects whose movement patterns vary significantly despite belonging to the same activity classes. Standard regularization techniques, such as weight decay, mitigate overfitting but do not explicitly constrain the geometric structure of learned representations. Recent theoretical work suggests that the singular value spectrum of weight matrices influences generalization, yet the specific impact of spectral entropy on subject-disjoint robustness remains unexplored.

Current literature establishes that time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. While substantial progress has been made in algorithmic responses, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking regarding the specific weight geometries that facilitate robustness [9]. Generalization bounds for autoregressive processes relate empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than sequences [10]. However, length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers with limited existing theoretical understanding [11]. Furthermore, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization in multi-label learning is still in the early stage, leaving open questions about how inductive biases impact performance [7]. However, accurate detection of generated content in low-entropy scenarios presents significant challenges, highlighting the complexity of managing entropy in learned systems [13, 16]. Despite these advances, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers.

This paper addresses this gap by testing whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. Our contributions are:

=== related_work ===
**Time Series and Out-of-Distribution Generalization**
Research on generalization in sequential and structured data highlights significant challenges regarding distribution shifts and model capacity. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking regarding the specific weight geometries that facilitate robustness [9]. Generalization bounds for autoregressive processes relate empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than sequences [10]. This perspective suggests that in-context learning can exploit task decomposition to learn efficiently, yet length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers with limited existing theoretical understanding [11]. Existing theoretical understanding of length generalization is limited, often providing only asymptotic results or focusing on specific problem classes [11]. Furthermore, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization in multi-label learning is still in the early stage, leaving open questions about how inductive biases impact performance [7]. How to reduce the dependency on the number of labels and quantitatively analyze the impact of various inductive biases in the generalization analysis of multi-label learning is still a crucial and open problem [7]. When training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting, indicating that standard regularization strategies may be insufficient [17]. Regularization based approaches to continual learning cannot learn to discriminate classes from different tasks in elemental continual benchmarks, highlighting shortcomings in current strategies [17].

**Entropy and Weight Structure in Regularization**
Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness. Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift [1]. Entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training has been investigated for calibrated confidence, but findings indicate it does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance [1]. Studies on latent variables suggest that the entropy of intermediate representations influences robustness to distributional shift, where removal of low-entropy bits can notably benefit out-of-distribution performance [5]. Conversely, top-entropy masking disproportionately harms performance both in-distribution and out-of-distribution, suggesting a complex relationship between entropy and utility [5]. Singular Bayesian neural networks argue that the parameter cost of standard Bayesian neural networks is often unnecessary when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay, proposing a low-rank parameterization [14]. This singularity captures structured weight correlations through shared latent factors, geometrically distinct from mean-field independence assumptions [14]. Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions of the training loss landscape, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood [2]. Additionally, empirical risk minimization is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning, necessitating richer algorithmic techniques [6]. The practice of machine learning is rife with considerably richer algorithmic techniques, perhaps the most notable of which is regularization, yet no such technique has broken away from the pack to characterize optimal learning in these general settings [6].

**Projections and Regularization Mechanisms**
Methods involving projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality and regularization. Reducing linear program sizes using random and data-driven projections accelerates solving, suggesting that learned projections can capture structure [3]. Learning projection matrices from data is beneficial, leading to significantly higher solution quality than existing random projection while greatly reducing solving time [3]. Regularization by denoising utilizes denoising engines as regularization strategies for inverse problems in image processing through fixed-point projection [12]. Reformulating regularization by denoising as a convex optimization problem utilizing a projection onto the fixed-point set of demicontractive denoisers provides guarantees for convergence [12]. Additionally, accurate detection of generated content in low-entropy scenarios presents significant challenges, highlighting the complexity of managing entropy in learned systems [13]. Unbiased watermarks face a tradeoff between watermark strength and the risk of unsatisfactory outputs in low-entropy scenarios [13]. Text watermarking presents significant challenges in low-entropy texts like code and mathematics, where tokens are hardly modifiable without changing intended meaning [16]. Existing research addresses this by relying on high-entropy tokens, yet detection accuracy remains suboptimal as they neglect strong watermark evidences embedded in low entropy tokens [16]. These works collectively underscore the difficulty of manipulating entropy structures without compromising utility, a tension central to the present study.

=== method ===
The core intervention in this study is the enforcement of a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights via a regularization term added to the training objective. This operator targets the geometry of the weight matrix directly, hypothesizing that concentrating energy into dominant temporal modes facilitates feature learning in finite-width networks. The term computes the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the weight matrix, normalizes singular values to probabilities, and minimizes their entropy. This encourages the model to select dominant temporal modes rather than distributing energy uniformly. The hypothesis posits that this spectral concentration enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay.

The comparator condition employs standard weight decay without the spectral entropy term. This baseline neutralizes the effect of weight magnitude regularization, isolating the contribution of spectral structure. By holding weight decay constant across conditions, any observed difference in held-out classification accuracy can be attributed to the spectral entropy minimization rather than overall parameter norm constraints. The first negative control involves entropy minimization applied to a fixed noise parameter, ruling out effects driven by the optimization landscape of the entropy term itself rather than the weight structure. The second negative control involves fixed noise without entropy optimization, ensuring that stochasticity in the training process does not confound the results.

The operator is the right expression of the hypothesis because it directly manipulates the singular value distribution, which theoretical work suggests influences generalization bounds. Singular Bayesian neural networks argue that weight matrices exhibiting fast singular value decay allow for low-rank parameterization, capturing structured weight correlations [14]. However, studies on latent variables suggest that low-entropy representations can hurt out-of-distribution performance, creating a tension this experiment resolves empirically [5]. The comparator neutralizes magnitude effects, ensuring that the spectral shape, not the scale, is the variable of interest. This design aligns with findings that sharpness-aware minimization improves generalization by steering parameters away from sharp regions, suggesting that landscape geometry matters [2].

The implementation computes the SVD at each training step for the input projection layer. The singular values are normalized to sum to one, forming a probability distribution. The entropy of this distribution is calculated and added to the loss function with a weighting coefficient. This process encourages the singular values to converge to a sparse distribution, effectively reducing the rank of the effective transformation. The baseline condition omits this term, relying solely on weight decay to constrain the weights. The negative controls apply the entropy term to non-weight parameters or fix the noise, isolating the mechanism. This setup ensures that any performance difference is due to the spectral constraint on the input projections specifically.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset. This dataset contains raw inertial signals organized into 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. We use the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. This split tests what this question asks because it ensures that the model must generalize to unseen subjects, simulating the distribution shift encountered in edge AI deployment. A random split would have hidden this challenge by allowing subject-specific features to leak into the training set, inflating accuracy estimates without proving robustness.

The model architecture is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear input projection (9 to 64 dimensions) and learned positional embedding (128 to 64 dimensions). It comprises 2 blocks, each with LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps, and feed-forward residuals. Training runs for 12 epochs with a batch size of 128 using SGD with learning rate 0.05 and momentum 0.9. The outcome definition is the number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. This metric directly measures the practical utility of the model in the target domain.

We employ 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Using this many seeds ensures that the results are not artifacts of specific initializations, providing statistical power to detect effects exceeding the worthwhile margin. Pairing every condition on one seed buys control over initialization variance, allowing paired statistical tests that are more sensitive to the intervention effect. The cost is increased computational budget, but this is necessary for a rigorous test of the hypothesis. The first negative control rules out optimization artifacts, and the second rules out stochasticity effects. Without these controls, it would be indistinguishable whether performance changes were due to the spectral constraint or the presence of any additional loss term. The analysis computes mean held-out classification accuracy with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for each condition.

We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, adhering to the preregistered analysis plan. Figure 1 displays the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the primary cohort. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0004419 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], paired randomisation p=0.75, Cohen's dz=0.05). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9053 [0.902, 0.908], while the baseline achieved 0.9049 [0.901, 0.908]. The first negative control and the second negative control both achieved 0.9049 [0.901, 0.908], performing comparably to the deterministic baseline.

The learning curves for the proposed condition and the baseline overlap substantially throughout training, visually confirming the lack of divergence in performance. This suggests that the spectral entropy minimization did not alter the optimization trajectory in a way that benefited generalization. The negative controls also track the baseline closely, indicating that the additional loss term did not introduce instability.

On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.002549 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], paired randomisation p=0.106, Cohen's dz=0.25). Again, the 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9087 [0.906, 0.912], while the baseline achieved 0.9061 [0.902, 0.91]. The negative controls both achieved 0.9061 [0.902, 0.91].

Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition in the replication cohort. Similar to the primary cohort, the learning curves overlap, with the proposed condition showing no consistent advantage over the baseline. The replication cohort confirms the primary result, reinforcing the conclusion that the intervention does not yield a worthwhile improvement. The effect size in the replication cohort (Cohen's dz=0.25) is slightly larger than in the primary cohort (0.05), but the confidence interval still spans zero, preventing a claim of significance. The consistency across cohorts suggests the null result is robust to seed variation.

=== discussion ===
The results indicate that minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections does not enhance feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. This finding contradicts the hypothesis that spectral concentration facilitates generalization in this regime. While prior work examines entropy maximization for weight noise robustness and singular value decay in Bayesian networks, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Our null result suggests that the mechanism proposed does not operate as anticipated in attention-based architectures.

This outcome aligns with findings that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance [1]. Although our intervention minimized rather than maximized entropy, the lack of benefit suggests that explicit entropy manipulation of weight structures is not a reliable path to robustness in this context. Studies on latent variables suggest that low-entropy representations can hurt out-of-distribution performance, which may explain why constraining the spectral entropy did not help [5]. The removal of low-entropy bits can notably benefit out-of-distribution performance, implying that diversity in representations is valuable [5]. Our intervention reduced spectral diversity, potentially limiting the model's capacity to adapt to subject-specific variations.

Singular Bayesian neural networks argue that weight matrices exhibiting fast singular value decay allow for low-rank parameterization, capturing structured weight correlations [14]. However, our results suggest that enforcing this structure via regularization does not translate to improved generalization accuracy on subject-disjoint data. The parameter cost savings observed in Bayesian contexts may not apply to deterministic transformers trained with SGD. Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood [2]. Our spectral entropy term may not have effectively steered the model away from sharp regions, or the landscape geometry may not be the primary driver of generalization in this task.

The consistency between primary and replication cohorts strengthens the validity of the null result. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cases, as the confidence intervals included zero. This highlights the importance of replication in distinguishing true effects from noise. The negative controls performed comparably to the baseline, ruling out confounding factors related to the optimization of the entropy term itself. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over spectral entropy minimization for robustness tasks in this regime. Future work should investigate whether spectral constraints are more effective in different architectures or domains, such as computer vision or language modeling, where weight structure may play a different role.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset and a specific Transformer architecture. The results may not generalize to other temporal domains or model families, such as recurrent neural networks or convolutional architectures. The spectral entropy minimization was applied only to the input projection weights; applying it to attention matrices or feed-forward layers might yield different results. The training budget was fixed at 12 epochs, and longer training schedules could potentially allow the regularization to take effect. The worthwhile margin was set at 0.0125098 proportion, which is stringent; smaller but practically relevant improvements might exist but remain undetected. Finally, the study focuses on subject-disjoint generalization, and the intervention might behave differently under other distribution shift scenarios, such as sensor drift or environmental changes.

=== conclusion ===
This study investigated whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks. The preregistered hypothesis predicted higher held-out classification accuracy exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Results from both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts were inconclusive, with confidence intervals including zero. The proposed condition did not outperform the baseline or negative controls. These findings indicate that minimizing spectral entropy of input projections does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. For someone choosing between these methods, standard weight decay remains the preferable choice due to its simplicity and equivalent performance. Future work should explore alternative geometric constraints or focus on domains where spectral structure is more critically linked to generalization.
