=== abstract ===
**Correction Notice:** Versions 2 and 3 of this manuscript incorporated textual corrections without formal erratum notices. Version 4 addresses editor feedback regarding the inertness of negative controls and includes this formal correction record.

Enforcing specific weight geometries is hypothesized to improve generalization in temporal feature learning, yet empirical evidence remains unsettled. This study tests whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, we evaluated the proposed condition across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75). The replication cohort showed a contrast of 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered margin. Both negative controls produced values bit-identical to the baseline, carrying no diagnostic information. These findings indicate that spectral entropy minimization on input projections does not reliably improve subject-disjoint generalization under these conditions. Practitioners should not expect gains exceeding the worthwhile margin from this intervention alone.

=== introduction ===
**Correction Notice:** This version (4) corrects the description of negative controls to reflect their inert implementation (bit-identical to baseline) and adds a formal erratum notice missing from versions 2 and 3, which corrected textual errors without notification.

Temporal feature learning in resource-constrained environments requires models that generalize robustly to unseen subjects. Distribution shifts and non-stationary dynamics frequently challenge out-of-distribution generalization in time series [9]. While standard regularization techniques like weight decay are ubiquitous, their efficacy in finite-width networks under subject-disjoint splits remains an open question. Specifically, the geometric properties of weight matrices that facilitate feature learning versus kernel regime behavior are not fully characterized. Prior work examines entropy maximization for weight noise robustness and singular value decay in Bayesian networks, but there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers.

This gap matters because clarifying the mechanistic role of weight spectra guides regularization design for edge AI where subject-disjoint robustness is critical. If low-entropy spectra concentrate energy into dominant temporal modes, models might learn more stable features. Conversely, if such constraints impair optimization, performance may degrade. Existing literature offers conflicting signals. Some studies suggest entropy maximization improves robustness [1], though recent audits indicate implementation failures in such claims [1]. Others argue low-entropy representations hurt out-of-distribution performance [5]. Still others propose that singular value decay allows for parameter efficiency without sacrificing calibration [14]. These disagreements motivate a boundary test of spectral entropy minimization in a controlled setting.

This paper reports a preregistered experiment testing the effect of spectral entropy minimization on input projection weights. We employ a subject-disjoint split to ensure evaluation reflects generalization to unseen individuals rather than random data partitions. The study utilizes a calibrated testbed with paired seeds to isolate the intervention's effect from stochastic variance. We distinguish between a primary cohort and a confirmatory-replication cohort to assess consistency.

Our contributions are:
- We execute a preregistered test of spectral entropy minimization on input projections in a subject-disjoint time-series task.
- We report separate outcomes for primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts without pooling.
- We document the inertness of negative controls implemented in the testbed.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report results honestly against this prediction, labeling unforeseen findings as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research on generalization in sequential and structured data highlights significant challenges regarding distribution shifts and model capacity. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. Generalization results for autoregressive processes relate empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than sequences [10]. Length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers with limited existing theoretical understanding, motivating auxiliary task frameworks [11]. Despite advances in algorithms, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization in multi-label learning is still in the early stage [7]. Furthermore, when training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting, highlighting regularization shortcomings [17]. These works collectively establish that standard empirical risk minimization often fails to characterize optimal learning in general settings, necessitating specialized regularization principles [6].

Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness. One study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training provides calibrated confidence under distribution shift [1]. However, that paper carries a retracted notice due to implementation discrepancies, limiting its evidentiary value [1]. Other research studies the relationship between the entropy of intermediate representations and a model's robustness to distributional shift, finding that low-entropy latent variables can hurt out-of-distribution performance [5]. In Bayesian contexts, singular value decay is argued to allow low-rank parameterization without unnecessary parameter costs [14]. Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions, though underlying mechanisms are debated [2]. Empirical risk minimization is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning, motivating principles like maximum entropy [6]. Additionally, accurate detection of generated content in low-entropy scenarios presents challenges, highlighting the complexity of entropy management in generation tasks [13]. Detection accuracy in low-entropy texts like code remains suboptimal without specialized detectors [16].

Methods involving projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality and regularization. Reducing linear program sizes using random and data-driven projections can accelerate solving while maintaining solution quality [3]. Denoising engines are utilized as regularization strategies for inverse problems through fixed-point projection, bridging theoretical gaps in Plug-and-Play priors [12]. These projection-based methods suggest that structured weight constraints can influence optimization trajectories. However, the specific impact of minimizing spectral entropy on input projections for temporal feature learning remains untested in subject-disjoint regimes.

This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific spectral constraint. Unlike entropy maximization for noise robustness [1], we test minimization for feature concentration. Unlike low-rank Bayesian parameterization [14], we operate on deterministic weights with a spectral penalty. Unlike sharpness-aware methods [2], we target the weight spectrum directly rather than the loss landscape geometry. The unsettled nature of entropy's role [5], [13] motivates our boundary test. We do not claim to resolve the theoretical debates but provide empirical evidence in a controlled setting. The failure of prior entropy-based claims [1] underscores the need for rigorous harness verification, which our design addresses through recorded activation counts, though as noted in the Correction Notice, the negative controls proved inert.

=== method ===
**Operator Specification.** The core intervention is the SpectralEntropyRegularization operator applied to the input projection weight matrix. This operator enforces a low-entropy singular value spectrum on the weights connecting input channels to the model's latent dimension. The hypothesis posits that concentrating energy into dominant singular modes facilitates temporal feature learning compared to distributing energy uniformly. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. Its term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, ensuring the combined objective is differentiated.

The algorithm retrieves the target parameter tensor $W$ of shape [64, 9]. It computes singular values $\sigma$ via SVD without computing unitary matrices. A sum $\sigma_{sum}$ is calculated with an epsilon safeguard of 1e-8 to prevent division by zero. Probabilities $p$ are normalized by dividing $\sigma$ by $\sigma_{sum}$. Entropy $H$ is computed as $-\sum(p \cdot \log(p + 1e-8))$. The loss term is scaled by a coefficient of 0.01 and returned to the harness. This term is non-negative and minimized when one singular value dominates. The operator contract fixes the ordering of singular values as descending and the normalization as probability summation.

**Comparator and Control.** The baseline condition serves as the control arm. It is defined by what the harness guarantees rather than a description of an intervention. Both the proposed condition and the baseline are trained from the same paired seed. This ensures dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step—the same forward pass, classification objective, backward pass, and optimizer update. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms. In the baseline condition, the intervention code takes its control branch: it adds no term to the training objective and leaves the target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. This design isolates the effect of the spectral entropy term.

**Gradient Handling.** The operator's term is added inside the autograd graph, so every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. Detaching a reference tensor inside a penalty stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. In the proposed condition, the spectral entropy term contributes to the gradient of the input projection weights. In the baseline, no such gradient contribution occurs. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point. If the control arm acted at any registered point, the experiment yields no result. This ensures the baseline reflects standard training without hidden modifications.

**Implementation.** One intervention implementation serves every arm. The harness tells the code which condition it is running in. The pseudocode describes the intervention arm, and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms. There is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state reaches evaluation. This separation ensures that measured outcomes reflect training dynamics rather than evaluation artifacts. The registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion derives from a versioned policy accuracy fraction. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve registered labels and report exclusions of the target magnitude separately.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The experimental design prioritizes validity in generalization claims over computational efficiency. We use a subject-disjoint split rather than a random split. A random split would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates through subject-specific memorization. The subject-disjoint split answers the question of whether the intervention helps the model learn features that transfer to unseen individuals. This is critical for edge AI deployment where new users are the target population. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus or sensor distribution.

**Pairing and Seeds.** We pair conditions by seed. Each seed generates a dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters used by both the proposed and baseline conditions. This pairing reduces variance in the contrast estimate by controlling for stochastic initialization and data ordering effects. We allocated 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. We never enumerate random seeds in the prose. The seed budget supports a planning target power of 90% for rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin.

**Negative Controls.** Two negative controls were registered to diagnose harness behavior. The first negative control computes spectral entropy on weights detached from the graph, preventing gradient flow. The second negative control was registered similarly. However, post-hoc audit revealed both negative controls were inert as implemented. They produced values bit-identical to the baseline on every seed in both cohorts. This means they carry no diagnostic information regarding harness bias or implementation correctness. We state this plainly to avoid misinterpretation. The recorded activity for these controls was zero, matching the baseline. This outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct; it only confirms the controls did not alter the objective.

**Analysis.** We report held-out classification accuracy as the primary metric. This is defined as the number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint test split. We use bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds. We distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects. The confirmatory cohort uses disjoint seeds but the same dataset split; it is not an independent replication on new data. We report primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately. We never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. The registered decision threshold determines significance. Where an outcome did not reach the threshold, we report it as measured without upgrading it with a verb of proof.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** Table 1 reports the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the primary cohort. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition achieved a mean of 0.9053 [0.9023, 0.9085]. The baseline condition achieved 0.9049 [0.9013, 0.9085]. The hypothesis-positive paired contrast was 0.0004419 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], paired randomisation p=0.75, Cohen's dz=0.05). The 95% CI includes zero. Therefore, there is no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The contrast did not exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Figure 2 visualizes these final metric values with confidence intervals. Figure 3 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps, indicating overlapping trajectories between the proposed and baseline conditions.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** Table 2 reports the results for the confirmatory-replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved a mean of 0.9087 [0.9057, 0.9116]. The baseline condition achieved 0.9061 [0.9022, 0.9099]. The hypothesis-positive paired contrast was 0.002549 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], paired randomisation p=0.106, Cohen's dz=0.25). The 95% CI includes zero. There is no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. While the point estimate is larger than in the primary cohort, the confidence interval still excludes the worthwhile margin. Figure 4 visualizes these values. Figure 5 shows the training trajectories, which remain closely aligned. We do not pool these cohorts. The confirmatory cohort is not an independent replication on new subjects; it uses new seeds on the same split.

**Negative Controls.** Both negative controls produced values bit-identical to the baseline on every seed in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, Negative control 1 and Negative control 2 both recorded 0.9049 [0.9013, 0.9085]. In the replication cohort, both recorded 0.9061 [0.9022, 0.9099]. This inertness means they carry no diagnostic information. We remove any statement that the controls validate the harness or the result. The registered primary contrast (proposed vs baseline) is unaffected by this finding, but the inability to diagnose harness bias via controls is a limitation. Figure 1 illustrates the experimental flow, showing where the operator applies the loss term. The recorded activity for controls was zero, consistent with the baseline harness behavior.

**Decision.** The preregistered hypothesis predicted the contrast would exceed 0.0125098. In neither cohort did the lower confidence bound exceed this margin. In the primary cohort, the CI spans zero. In the replication cohort, the CI spans zero. We preserve the registered label of inconclusive. A CI crossing zero but lying below the worthwhile margin excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. The results do not support the claim that spectral entropy minimization enhances feature learning in this setting.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that spectral entropy minimization on input projections did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy exceeding the preregistered margin. The outcome was inconclusive in both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts. This suggests that enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum does not reliably enhance feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay under these conditions. The measured outcome licenses a decision to not adopt this intervention for the goal of exceeding the 0.0125098 margin in similar subject-disjoint settings.

**Mechanism and Alternatives.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings. We named the directly recorded outcomes (accuracy) and do not claim attention stability or feature learning from an accuracy contrast alone. One hypothesis is that low-entropy spectra concentrate energy into dominant temporal modes. An alternative is that the penalty constrains optimization too severely, preventing the model from adapting to subject-specific variations. The inert negative controls prevent us from ruling out harness implementation issues definitively, though the baseline activity was recorded as zero. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; we did not measure attention maps. The small coefficient (0.01) alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient.

**Comparison to Literature.** These findings stand in contrast to claims that entropy maximization improves robustness [1], though that paper is retracted and thus not comparable evidence. Our results align with findings that low-entropy latent variables can hurt out-of-distribution performance [5], suggesting that constraining entropy may limit representational capacity needed for generalization. Unlike Singular Bayesian Neural Networks which argue for low-rank parameterization [14], we operated on full-rank weights with a spectral penalty. The lack of improvement contrasts with Sharpness-Aware Minimization results [2], implying that spectral entropy is not a sufficient proxy for flatness in this regime. Generalization bounds for autoregressive processes relate loss to denoising [10], but our spectral penalty does not explicitly target denoising loss.

**Replication Value.** The confirmatory-replication cohort adds consistency to the null finding. Both cohorts showed inconclusive results with CIs spanning zero. The replication cohort showed a slightly larger point estimate (0.002549 vs 0.0004419), but the uncertainty remained too high to claim success. This consistency suggests the effect, if any, is smaller than the worthwhile margin. The confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication; it uses the same dataset split. Thus, we cannot claim generalization to new datasets or sensors.

**Next Steps.** To settle the question, future work should test the intervention on new datasets and architectures. Direct measurement of the weight spectrum during training would clarify if the penalty successfully altered the geometry. Independent replication on new subjects would strengthen generalization claims. Until then, the finding remains specific to the UCI HAR dataset and this Transformer architecture.

=== limitations ===
**Control Inertness.** A critical limitation is that both negative controls were inert as implemented. They produced values bit-identical to the baseline on every seed in both cohorts. This means they carry no diagnostic information. We cannot use them to validate the harness or prove the implementation correct. This limits our ability to rule out subtle implementation biases that affect both arms equally.

**Design Scope.** The design evaluates generalization to unseen subjects within the same dataset distribution. It does not establish out-of-distribution generalization to different sensors, activities, or environments. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus. The confirmatory cohort uses disjoint seeds but the same split; it is not an independent replication on new data.

**Power and Margin.** The registered power calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. The inconclusive result may reflect insufficient power to detect small effects, though the effect sizes (dz=0.05, dz=0.25) suggest the true effect is likely small.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether spectral entropy minimization of input projections enhances feature learning in subject-disjoint time-series tasks. The results were inconclusive in both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts. The proposed condition did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Negative controls were inert and carried no diagnostic information. These findings indicate that this specific regularization does not reliably improve generalization under these conditions. Practitioners should not expect gains exceeding the margin from this intervention alone. Future work should measure weight spectra directly and test on new datasets to settle the question of spectral geometry in temporal feature learning.

If spectral concentration facilitates feature learning, it could offer a principled alternative to heuristic decay schedules. Conversely, if spectral entropy is irrelevant to held-out accuracy in this regime, computational resources spent enforcing it are wasted. This paper reports a calibrated testbed experiment designed to isolate the effect of spectral entropy minimization on input projection weights. We compare a proposed condition enforcing low-entropy singular values against a baseline of standard weight decay.

The combined objective is differentiated, ensuring the operator-owned parameters are trained by it.

A random split would allow windows from the same subject to appear in both training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates through subject-specific signal leakage. The official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset ensures that the 2,947 held-out windows come from subjects unseen during training, answering the question of robustness to new users rather than just new windows. This distinction is critical for edge AI deployment where model users differ from the training population.

**Pairing and Variance.** Conditions are paired by seed to reduce variance in the contrast estimate. By deriving dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters once and reusing them by both arms, we isolate the effect of the spectral entropy term from stochastic training variation. This pairing allows for a paired randomisation test, which is more sensitive to small effects than an unpaired test given the high correlation between seeds. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides sufficient power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin, assuming the planning SD holds.

**Control Interpretation.** The registered negative controls were intended to isolate the effect of gradient flow through the entropy term. Negative control 1, computing entropy on detached weights, was designed to test whether the mere calculation of the metric (without backpropagation) influenced results via side channels. However, as noted in the Method, both negative controls were inert as implemented, producing values bit-identical to the baseline. This observation limits our ability to rule out implementation artifacts via control contrasts. The observed contrast between the proposed condition and baseline therefore rests solely on the primary intervention's recorded activity, without diagnostic support from the controls. The analysis treats the control arms as defining the null distribution for the baseline, but does not claim they validate the absence of bias in the harness.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** In the primary cohort, across 43 seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9053 (95% CI [0.9023, 0.9085]). The baseline condition achieved 0.9049 (95% CI [0.9013, 0.9085]). The hypothesis-positive paired contrast was 0.0004419 proportion (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], paired randomisation p=0.75, Cohen's dz=0.05). As shown in Figure 1, the confidence interval for the contrast includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive; the result does not reject the zero-effect null, nor does the lower confidence bound exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. Figure 2 illustrates the training trajectory, showing overlapping accuracy curves between the proposed and baseline conditions throughout the 12 epochs.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 43 disjoint seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9087 (95% CI [0.9057, 0.9116]). The baseline condition achieved 0.9061 (95% CI [0.9022, 0.9099]). The hypothesis-positive paired contrast was 0.002549 proportion (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], paired randomisation p=0.106, Cohen's dz=0.25). Figure 3 displays the final metric values with confidence intervals, again showing overlap between conditions. Figure 4 shows the training steps, where the proposed condition tracks the baseline closely. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. While the mean contrast is larger than in the primary cohort, the 95% CI still includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered margin.

**Control Outcomes.** The negative controls produced values bit-identical to the baseline in both cohorts. Table 1 and Table 2 report the condition means; the negative control rows match the baseline rows exactly (0.9049 in primary, 0.9061 in replication). This identity confirms the inert implementation described in the Method and Limitations. No statistical contrast exists between the controls and the baseline, as the values are identical. The registered primary contrast (proposed vs baseline) is unaffected by this control status, but the lack of diagnostic variation in the controls precludes using them to rule out harness bias.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that spectral entropy minimization on input projections did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The observed contrasts (0.0004419 and 0.002549) are small relative to the registered worthwhile margin (0.0125098), and their confidence intervals include zero. This outcome is inconsistent with the hypothesis that low-entropy spectra enhance feature learning in this regime.

**Interpretation.** This result suggests that, for this architecture and dataset, the singular value distribution of input projections is not a primary driver of subject-disjoint generalization. The mechanism hypothesized—that concentrating energy into dominant temporal modes improves robustness—did not manifest in the accuracy metric. It is possible that the regularization coefficient (0.01) was too small to alter the optimization trajectory meaningfully, or that the transformer's self-attention mechanism already manages spectral distribution implicitly. Alternatively, the capacity of the network (64-dimensional embeddings) may be sufficient to learn robust features without explicit spectral constraints.

**Relation to Literature.** These findings contrast with claims that entropy maximization improves robustness, though Reference [1] supporting that view is retracted. They align more closely with findings that low-entropy latent variables can hurt out-of-distribution performance [5], suggesting that enforcing low entropy (the opposite of [5]'s removal of low-entropy bits) may not confer benefit. The result also fails to support the singular Bayesian neural network argument that fast singular value decay is beneficial [14], at least in this deterministic, finite-width setting. Unlike Sharpness-Aware Minimization, which steers parameters away from sharp regions [2], spectral entropy minimization targets weight geometry directly, which appears less impactful for generalization here.

**Replication Value.** The confirmatory replication cohort adds precision to the estimate but does not change the qualitative conclusion. The contrast increased slightly in replication, but the uncertainty remains too high to claim an effect exceeding the margin. This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if any, is smaller than the worthwhile threshold.

**Mechanistic Alternatives.** An alternative explanation for the null result is that the spectral entropy term is orthogonal to the features required for activity recognition. Inertial signals may rely on temporal patterns that do not correlate with the singular value spread of the input projection. Future work measuring the actual singular value spectra during training would clarify whether the operator successfully modified the weights without affecting accuracy.

=== limitations ===
**Inert Controls.** A critical limitation is that both negative controls were inert as implemented. They produced values bit-identical to the baseline on every seed in both cohorts. Consequently, they carry no diagnostic information. We cannot use them to validate that the harness is unbiased or that the implementation of the proposed condition is correct beyond the recorded activity logs. This limits our ability to rule out subtle implementation artifacts that might affect both proposed and baseline arms equally.

**Design Scope.** The study is limited to a single dataset (UCI HAR) and architecture (PreNormTransformerEncoder). While the subject-disjoint split supports claims about unseen subjects, it does not establish domain generalization to different sensors or activities. The registered power calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin; it does not guarantee power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. Thus, the inconclusive classification reflects both statistical uncertainty and the stringency of the margin criterion.

=== conclusion ===
This study found no evidence that spectral entropy minimization of input projection weights enhances subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The preregistered hypothesis was not supported; the measured contrasts were inconclusive in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. For practitioners choosing between these methods, the results license the use of standard weight decay, as the spectral intervention offers no measured accuracy benefit. Future work should investigate whether larger regularization coefficients or different architectural bottlenecks activate the hypothesized mechanism, and must ensure negative controls are functionally active to validate the experimental harness.

=== correction_note ===
**Correction Note.** This version (v4) supersedes versions 2 and 3. Version 2 corrected reference formatting errors in the Related Work section. Version 3 corrected labeling errors in the cohort descriptions within the Results section. Both previous corrections were issued without an accompanying erratum notice. This version (v4) includes this formal correction note and clarifies the operational status of the negative controls, which were found to be inert (bit-identical to the baseline) across all seeds. No changes have been made to the primary results or the preregistered analysis plan.

=== abstract ===
This study investigates whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. Clarifying the mechanistic role of weight spectra in generalization is critical for regularization design in resource-constrained edge AI where subject-disjoint robustness is critical. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 proportion (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort showed a contrast of 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106). Both confidence intervals include zero and fail to exceed the preregistered margin. Negative controls were inert, producing values bit-identical to the baseline. These findings indicate no evidence that spectral entropy minimization of input projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. Practitioners should not prioritize this specific regularization over standard weight decay for robustness tasks in this setting.

=== introduction ===
**The Problem of Weight Geometry in Temporal Learning.** Deep learning models for sequential data often rely on regularization techniques to prevent overfitting and improve generalization to unseen distributions. Standard practices, such as weight decay, penalize the magnitude of parameters but do not explicitly constrain the geometric structure of the weight matrices. In temporal tasks, where input projections map raw sensor signals into latent representations, the singular value spectrum of these weights may influence how temporal modes are captured. If the energy of the projection is distributed uniformly across singular values, the model may operate in a kernel-like regime, whereas a low-entropy spectrum might encourage the selection of dominant temporal features. === method ===
**Operator Specification.** The experiment employs the SpectralEntropyRegularization operator applied to the input_proj.weight parameter. This operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The singular values are sorted descending by the SVD routine. Probabilities sum to 1 via division by the sum of singular values. Numerical safeguards include an epsilon of 1e-8 added to the sum and log argument to prevent division by zero and log(0).

**Algorithm 1: SpectralEntropyRegularization.**
1. Retrieve target parameter tensor W (shape [64, 9]).
2. Compute singular values sigma = svd(W, compute_uv=False).
3. Compute sum_sigma = sum(sigma) + 1e-8.
4. Normalize probabilities p = sigma / sum_sigma.
5. Compute entropy H = -sum(p * log(p + 1e-8)).
6. Scale term: loss_term = 0.01 * H.
7. Return loss_term to harness for addition to objective.

The following invariants hold throughout: H is non-negative; H is maximized when all singular values are equal; H is minimized when one singular value dominates.

**Hypothesis Alignment.** This operator directly expresses the hypothesis that enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum enhances feature learning. By minimizing H, the regularization encourages the model to select dominant temporal modes rather than distributing energy uniformly. The registered comparator holds fixed the standard training objective without this term. The control arm is the same code taking its control branch, adding no term to the training objective and leaving the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition.

**Implementation Details.** The intervention implementation serves every arm. The harness tells it which condition it is running in. In the control arm, the intervention returns immediately, adding no term. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. This design ensures that any observed difference in accuracy is attributable to the training dynamics induced by the regularization term.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The experiment uses the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. This split answers the question of robustness to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. A random split would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates and masking failures in generalization. The subject-disjoint split ensures that the held-out evaluation measures performance on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects.

**Pairing and Controls.** Conditions are paired by seed. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing reduces variance due to initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The registered negative controls were intended to diagnose harness bias. The first negative control computes spectral entropy on W detached from the graph (no gradient flow). The second negative control was registered similarly. However, both negative controls were inert as implemented: they produced values bit-identical to the baseline on every seed in both cohorts. This means they carry no diagnostic information. We state this plainly to remove any statement that the controls validate the harness or the result. The registered primary contrast (proposed vs baseline) is unaffected by this inertness, but the controls cannot rule out implementation bias.

**Seed Budget and Analysis.** The experiment uses 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. This budget was chosen to achieve 90% planning target power with a planning SD of 0.0250196 and a registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. We report both cohorts separately and never pool them.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 1 and Figure 2). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0004419 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], paired randomisation p=0.75, Cohen's dz=0.05). There was no statistically significant difference because the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9053 [0.902, 0.908], while the baseline achieved 0.9049 [0.901, 0.908]. The negative controls matched the baseline exactly at 0.9049 [0.901, 0.908]. Figure 3 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps, indicating overlapping trajectories.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 2 and Figure 4). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.002549 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], paired randomisation p=0.106, Cohen's dz=0.25). There was no statistically significant difference because the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9087 [0.906, 0.912], while the baseline achieved 0.9061 [0.902, 0.91]. The negative controls matched the baseline exactly at 0.9061 [0.902, 0.91]. Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for this cohort.

**Interpretation of Results.** Both cohorts failed to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The confidence intervals in both cases include zero and lie below the margin. This preserves the registered label of inconclusive. We separately explain that the CI excludes gains of the target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The replication cohort did not confirm the primary result as positive; both are null with respect to the hypothesis. The inertness of the negative controls is visible in the identical means and intervals for the baseline and control conditions.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that spectral entropy minimization of input projection weights did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay. The observed contrasts were small (0.0004419 in primary, 0.002549 in replication) and the confidence intervals included zero. This outcome is inconclusive with respect to the preregistered hypothesis. It does not prove equality, but it fails to support the claim that low-entropy spectra enhance feature learning in this setting.

**Mechanism and Alternatives.** The hypothesis rested on the rationale that minimizing spectral entropy encourages the model to select dominant temporal modes. An alternative explanation for the null result is that the regularization coefficient (0.01) was too small to alter the optimization trajectory meaningfully. Another alternative is that the subject-disjoint shift in UCI HAR is not sensitive to input projection spectra, but rather to higher-level attention mechanisms. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. We did not measure attention stability or feature learning directly, so we cannot claim them from an accuracy contrast alone.

**Relation to Cited Work.** These findings contrast with the retracted claims of [1], which suggested entropy maximization might improve robustness (though that paper was retracted for implementation errors). Our null result aligns more closely with [5], which found that low-entropy latent variables can hurt out-of-distribution performance, suggesting that constraining entropy may not always aid generalization. However, [14] argues that singular value decay can reduce parameter costs, which is a different objective than accuracy improvement. Our result does not contradict [14] because we did not measure parameter efficiency. The findings also stand alongside [2], which shows generalization aware minimization improves performance, suggesting that sharpness-aware methods may be more effective than spectral entropy constraints.

**Replication Value.** The confirmatory-replication cohort adds value by showing that the null result is stable across disjoint seeds. The replication contrast was slightly larger than the primary (0.002549 vs 0.0004419), but still inconclusive. This consistency suggests the effect size is likely small or zero in this regime. The confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication of the primary data, but it tests the robustness of the finding to new random seeds.

**Conclusion on Evidence.** The measured outcome licenses a conclusion that there is no evidence for benefit. It does not license a claim that the method is harmful, as the CIs include zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the results suggest standard weight decay is sufficient, as the added complexity of spectral entropy minimization did not pay off.

**Inert Negative Controls.** A key limitation is that both negative controls were inert as implemented. They produced values bit-identical to the baseline on every seed in both cohorts. This means they carry no diagnostic information. We cannot use them to validate the harness or the result. The registered primary contrast is unaffected, but we cannot rule out implementation bias using these controls.

**Design Scope.** The design uses a subject-disjoint split on UCI HAR. This supports a claim about unseen subjects but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. We do not call this out-of-distribution or domain generalisation beyond the subject split. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter.

=== conclusion ===
This study found no evidence that enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. The preregistered hypothesis was not supported in either the primary or confirmatory-replication cohorts, with both contrasts failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. payload.content:
=== abstract ===
This study investigates whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. While prior work examines entropy maximization for robustness and singular value decay in Bayesian networks, the effect of spectral entropy minimization on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains unexplored. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Using a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort showed a contrast of 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106). Both confidence intervals include zero and fail to exceed the registered margin. Negative controls were inert, carrying no diagnostic information. We conclude that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not demonstrate a measurable benefit over standard weight decay in this regime.

Correction Note: This manuscript supersedes Versions 2 and 3, which incorporated prior editorial corrections without formal erratum. This version corrects the description of negative controls (which were inert), updates reference formatting to remove OpenReview-only identifiers, and clarifies confidence interval reporting.

=== introduction ===
Temporal feature learning in resource-constrained environments requires models that generalize robustly to unseen subjects. Deep learning architectures, particularly transformers, have achieved significant success in processing sequential data, yet their generalization mechanisms under distribution shift remain partially understood. A critical open problem is identifying the specific weight geometry that facilitates feature learning versus kernel regime behavior in finite-width networks. Standard regularization techniques, such as weight decay, penalize parameter magnitude but do not explicitly constrain the spectral structure of weight matrices. This gap leaves open the question of whether shaping the singular value distribution of input projections can improve subject-disjoint robustness.

Current literature offers conflicting perspectives on the role of entropy and weight structure in generalization. Some studies suggest that maximizing entropy in weight noise parameters improves calibrated confidence under distribution shift [1], while others argue that low-entropy latent variables hurt out-of-distribution performance [5]. In the context of Bayesian neural networks, fast singular value decay has been proposed as a means to reduce parameter cost while maintaining performance [14]. However, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. This uncertainty hinders the design of regularization strategies for edge AI, where subject-disjoint robustness is critical.

This paper presents a calibrated testbed experiment to address this gap. We test the hypothesis that enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. The intervention adds a regularization term to the training objective that computes the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the input projection weight matrix, normalizes singular values to probabilities, and minimizes their entropy. This encourages the model to select dominant temporal modes rather than distributing energy uniformly. We evaluate this intervention on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using an official subject-disjoint split, ensuring that held-out evaluation measures generalization to unseen subjects rather than unseen windows from trained subjects.

The contributions of this work are as follows:
- We implement and evaluate a spectral entropy minimization operator on input projections within a transformer architecture for time-series classification.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a confirmatory-replication cohort, adhering to preregistered decision rules regarding the worthwhile margin.
- We provide empirical evidence regarding the impact of weight spectral geometry on subject-disjoint generalization, finding no significant benefit over standard weight decay.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results honestly against this prediction, labeling any unforeseen finding as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research on generalization in sequential and structured data highlights significant challenges regarding distribution shifts and model capacity. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. Generalization bounds for autoregressive processes relate empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than sequences [10]. Length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers, with limited theoretical understanding of how to guarantee performance on sequences longer than those encountered during training [11]. Additionally, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization in multi-label learning is still in the early stage, despite algorithmic advances [7]. When training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting, and regularization-based approaches have shown shortcomings in continual learning scenarios [17].

Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness. One study investigated whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training provides calibrated confidence under distribution shift [1]. That work, now retracted due to implementation discrepancies, refuted the hypothesis that entropy maximization improves accuracy in attention-based architectures [1]. Conversely, other research studies the relationship between the entropy of intermediate representations and a model's robustness to distributional shift, finding that low-entropy latent variables can hurt out-of-distribution performance [5]. In Bayesian neural networks, it is argued that the parameter cost of standard posteriors is often unnecessary when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay, proposing low-rank parameterization to capture structured weight correlations [14]. Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions of the training loss landscape, though the underlying mechanisms are debated [2]. Furthermore, empirical risk minimization is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning, motivating the search for optimal regularization principles [6].

Methods involving projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality and regularization. Research explores reducing linear program sizes using random and data-driven projections to accelerate solving, showing that learning projection matrices from data can lead to higher solution quality [3]. In image processing, denoising engines are utilized as regularization strategies for inverse problems through fixed-point projection, bridging theoretical gaps between different frameworks [12]. While these methods address projection and regularization in different domains, they motivate the investigation of spectral properties in neural network weights. Specifically, the question of whether minimizing spectral entropy in input projections facilitates feature learning versus kernel regime behavior remains unsettled. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific spectral constraint in a subject-disjoint temporal setting, distinguishing our intervention from entropy maximization [1] and low-rank Bayesian approaches [14].

=== method ===
The core of this study is the Spectral Entropy Minimization operator applied to the input projection weights of a transformer encoder. The hypothesis posits that concentrating the singular value spectrum of the input projection matrix enhances the model's ability to learn dominant temporal modes, thereby improving generalization to unseen subjects. This operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step, adding a regularization term to the classification objective inside the autograd graph. The combined objective is differentiated, ensuring the operator-owned parameters are trained by the spectral penalty.

The operator targets the `input_proj.weight` tensor, which maps the 9-channel inertial input to the 64-dimensional model embedding. By minimizing the entropy of the singular values, the intervention encourages a low-rank structure where a few dominant singular values capture most of the variance. This contrasts with standard weight decay, which penalizes the L2 norm of weights without regard for their spectral distribution. The rationale is that a low-entropy spectrum may prevent the model from distributing energy uniformly across all input channels, potentially reducing noise sensitivity in resource-constrained edge AI deployments.

The registered comparator is the baseline condition, which employs standard weight decay without the spectral entropy term. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, ensuring that dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm, the intervention adds no term to the training objective and leaves the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged.

The operator specification is fixed before any compute was spent. The singular values are sorted descending by the SVD routine. Probabilities sum to 1 via division by the sum of singular values, with an epsilon of 1e-8 added to the sum and log argument to prevent division by zero and log(0). The entropy term is scaled by a coefficient of 0.01. This specification ensures that the penalty is non-negative and minimized when one singular value dominates. The control arm logic ensures that any observed contrast is attributable to the operator's activity, as the harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

**Registered Operator Specification**
SpectralEntropyRegularization is applied to `input_proj.weight`.
- Scope: Singular value distribution of the weight matrix.
- Applied: The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step.
- Ordering: Singular values sorted descending by SVD routine.
- Normalisation: Probabilities sum to 1 via division by sum of singular values.
- Numerical safeguards: Epsilon 1e-8 added to sum and log argument.

Algorithm 1:
1. Retrieve target parameter tensor W (shape [64, 9]).

The principal finding of this study is that spectral entropy minimization of input projection weights does not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint temporal setting. === introduction ===
Temporal feature learning in resource-constrained environments requires models that generalize robustly to unseen subjects. Deep learning architectures, particularly transformers, have achieved significant success in processing sequential data, yet their generalization mechanisms under distribution shift remain partially understood. A critical open problem is identifying the specific weight geometry that facilitates feature learning versus kernel regime behavior in finite-width networks. Standard regularization techniques, such as weight decay, penalize parameter magnitude but do not explicitly constrain the spectral structure of weight matrices. This gap leaves open the question of whether shaping the singular value distribution of input projections can improve subject-disjoint robustness.

Current literature offers conflicting perspectives on the role of entropy and weight structure in generalization. Some studies suggest that maximizing entropy in weight noise parameters improves calibrated confidence under distribution shift [1], while others argue that low-entropy latent variables hurt out-of-distribution performance [5]. In the context of Bayesian neural networks, fast singular value decay has been proposed as a means to reduce parameter cost while maintaining performance [14]. However, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. This uncertainty hinders the design of regularization strategies for edge AI, where subject-disjoint robustness is critical.

This paper presents a calibrated testbed experiment to address this gap. We test the hypothesis that enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. The intervention adds a regularization term to the training objective that computes the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the input projection weight matrix, normalizes singular values to probabilities, and minimizes their entropy. This encourages the model to select dominant temporal modes rather than distributing energy uniformly. We evaluate this intervention on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using an official subject-disjoint split, ensuring that held-out evaluation measures generalization to unseen subjects rather than unseen windows from trained subjects.

The contributions of this work are as follows:
- We implement and evaluate a spectral entropy minimization operator on input projections within a transformer architecture for time-series classification.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a confirmatory-replication cohort, adhering to preregistered decision rules regarding the worthwhile margin.
- We provide empirical evidence regarding the impact of weight spectral geometry on subject-disjoint generalization, finding no significant benefit over standard weight decay.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results honestly against this prediction, labeling any unforeseen finding as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research on generalization in sequential and structured data highlights significant challenges regarding distribution shifts and model capacity. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. Generalization bounds for autoregressive processes relate empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than sequences [10]. Length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers, with limited theoretical understanding of how to guarantee performance on sequences longer than those encountered during training [11]. Additionally, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization in multi-label learning is still in the early stage, despite algorithmic advances [7]. When training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting, and regularization-based approaches have shown shortcomings in continual learning scenarios [17].

Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness. One study investigated whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training provides calibrated confidence under distribution shift [1]. That work, now retracted due to implementation discrepancies, refuted the hypothesis that entropy maximization improves accuracy in attention-based architectures [1]. Conversely, other research studies the relationship between the entropy of intermediate representations and a model's robustness to distributional shift, finding that low-entropy latent variables can hurt out-of-distribution performance [5]. In Bayesian neural networks, it is argued that the parameter cost of standard posteriors is often unnecessary when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay, proposing low-rank parameterization to capture structured weight correlations [14]. Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions of the training loss landscape, though the underlying mechanisms are debated [2]. Furthermore, empirical risk minimization is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning, motivating the search for optimal regularization principles [6].

While these methods address projection and regularization in different domains, they motivate the investigation of spectral properties in neural network weights. Specifically, the question of whether minimizing spectral entropy in input projections facilitates feature learning versus kernel regime behavior remains unsettled. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific spectral constraint in a subject-disjoint temporal setting, distinguishing our intervention from entropy maximization [1] and low-rank Bayesian approaches [14].
