payload.content:
=== abstract ===
Spectral entropy minimization of input projections is proposed to enhance feature learning in temporal transformers by encouraging dominant temporal modes over uniform energy distribution. This study tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights improves subject-disjoint generalization compared to standard weight decay. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Using a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort showed a contrast of 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106). Both confidence intervals include zero, failing to reject the zero-effect null or exceed the registered margin. Negative controls were inert and carry no diagnostic information. These findings indicate that spectral entropy minimization of input weights does not reliably enhance subject-disjoint robustness in this regime. Practitioners should not expect accuracy gains from this specific spectral regularization without further evidence.

=== introduction ===
Correction Note: Version 2 corrected reference identifiers from OpenReview to arXiv/DOI where available. Version 3 corrected the description of negative control implementation to reflect their inert status. Version 4 (this revision) clarifies that inert controls cannot validate the harness and updates the citation status of [1] to reflect retraction.

Temporal feature learning in resource-constrained edge AI requires models that generalize robustly to unseen subjects. Distribution shifts and non-stationary dynamics in time-series data frequently challenge out-of-distribution generalization, particularly when training and deployment populations differ [6]. Standard regularization techniques, such as weight decay, constrain parameter magnitude but do not explicitly shape the spectral geometry of weight matrices. Theoretical work suggests that weight spectra influence whether networks operate in a feature-learning regime versus a kernel regime, yet empirical evidence linking specific spectral properties to subject-disjoint robustness remains unsettled. While prior work examines entropy maximization for weight noise robustness and singular value decay in Bayesian networks, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers.

This gap matters because clarifying the mechanistic role of weight spectra in generalization guides regularization design for edge AI where subject-disjoint robustness is critical. If low-entropy spectra facilitate feature learning by selecting dominant temporal modes, this could offer a targeted inductive bias for sequential data. Conversely, if spectral entropy minimization yields no benefit, resources should focus on alternative architectural or optimization strategies. This paper reports a preregistered experiment testing whether spectral entropy minimization of input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay.

We address the open problem of what specific weight geometry facilitates feature learning versus kernel regime behavior in finite-width networks. Our study isolates the effect of spectral entropy regularization on the input projection layer of a transformer encoder, holding all other architectural and optimization factors constant. We evaluate performance on held-out subjects to ensure claims about generalization reflect subject-disjoint robustness rather than random split variance.

The contributions of this work are:
- We execute a preregistered test of spectral entropy minimization on input projections in a time-series transformer, reporting both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts.
- We provide exact quantitative estimates of the effect size with 95% confidence intervals, determining whether the effect exceeds a registered worthwhile margin.
- We document the inertness of registered negative controls, clarifying their inability to validate the experimental harness.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report results honestly against this prediction, labeling any unforeseen finding as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research on generalization in sequential and structured data highlights significant challenges regarding distribution shifts and model capacity. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [6]. This motivates the use of subject-disjoint evaluation splits to assess robustness to unseen populations rather than random data partitions. When training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting and regularization strategies may fail to discriminate classes from different tasks [8]. This underscores the need for regularization techniques that explicitly account for the geometry of learned representations in non-iid settings.

Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness. Entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters was investigated to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift, but results refuted the hypothesis that it improves out-of-distribution accuracy in attention-based architectures [1]. This suggests that explicit entropy maximization may actively impair performance in this regime. Conversely, studies on latent variables indicate that low-entropy intermediate representations can hurt out-of-distribution performance, as removing low-entropy bits may benefit robustness [4]. This presents a tension: while low-entropy latents may harm OOD performance, we test whether low-entropy *weights* facilitate feature selection. The relationship between entropy and robustness thus depends on whether entropy is measured in activations or parameters, and whether it is maximized or minimized.

Regularization theory notes that empirical risk minimization is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning [5]. Regularization principles, such as structural risk minimization, are required to characterize optimal learning in multiclass settings. This supports the investigation of spectral regularization as a means to steer optimization towards flatter or more structured minima. However, the specific impact of singular value entropy on the input projection layer remains untested in transformer-based time-series models.

Methods involving projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality and regularization, though often in linear programming contexts. While data-driven projections can accelerate solving linear programs and improve solution quality [2], their extension to neural network weight spectra requires empirical validation. The gap this work addresses is that while prior work examines entropy maximization for weight noise robustness and singular value decay in Bayesian networks, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We position this study against the themes of spectral geometry and entropy-based regularization, testing whether minimizing spectral entropy in input weights aligns with the feature-learning hypothesis in a subject-disjoint setting.

=== method ===
The method centers on the Spectral Entropy Minimization operator applied to the input projection weights. The hypothesis posits that enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum enhances feature learning by encouraging the model to select dominant temporal modes rather than distributing energy uniformly. This operator is the registered intervention, and its comparator holds all other training dynamics fixed.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. Its term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The scope is the singular value distribution of the weight matrix. Specifically, the operator retrieves the target parameter tensor W (shape [64, 9]), computes singular values sigma via SVD, and normalizes them to probabilities p by dividing by their sum plus an epsilon safeguard. It then computes entropy H as the negative sum of p times log(p). The loss term is scaled by a coefficient of 0.01 and returned to the harness for addition to the objective. This formulation ensures H is non-negative and minimized when one singular value dominates.

The registered comparator is the baseline condition, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective.

The registered negative controls were intended to isolate specific implementation artifacts. The first negative control computes spectral entropy on W detached from the graph, preventing gradient flow. This was intended to test whether the gradient signal from the entropy term, rather than the term's value, drives any observed effect. However, as noted in the Limitations, both negative controls were inert as implemented. The method focuses on the operator's mathematical expression of the hypothesis: that minimizing spectral entropy on input projections shapes the weight geometry to favor dominant temporal modes. We do not claim attention stability or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone; the measured outcome is held-out classification accuracy.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design prioritizes subject-disjoint generalization over random-split performance. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of robustness to unseen individuals, which a random split would not, as random splits allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing. This design choice ensures that claims about generalization reflect performance on new subjects, not merely interpolation within a subject's data distribution. Variation is attributed to seeds, not subjects, as the experimental unit is the seeded training run.

Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance by ensuring both arms see the same data ordering and initialization. This allows for paired statistical tests that are more sensitive to small effects than unpaired tests. The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication in the sense of new subjects or datasets; it is a replication on new seeds within the same subject-disjoint split. This distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects or architectures.

The negative controls' intended alternative explanation was to verify that any observed effect stemmed from the gradient signal of the entropy term rather than computational artifacts. The first negative control detached the weight tensor from the graph. However, the observed contrast supports no diagnostic conclusion because both negative controls were inert as implemented: bit-identical to the baseline on every seed in both cohorts. This inertness means they carry no diagnostic information and cannot validate the harness or the implementation. The registered primary contrast is unaffected by this inertness but remains inconclusive based on the measured outcomes. The analysis uses bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds to quantify uncertainty, preserving registered labels without equating nonsignificance with equality.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, stating each preregistered decision. We never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. Figure 1 illustrates the flow from UCI HAR data through the PreNormTransformerEncoder, applying SpectralEntropyRegularization to input_proj.weight at the loss term across registered arms. Figure 2 and Figure 4 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. Figure 3 and Figure 5 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

In the primary cohort, across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0004419 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], paired randomisation p=0.75, Cohen's dz=0.05). There is no statistically significant difference because the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9053 [0.9023, 0.9085], while the baseline achieved 0.9049 [0.9013, 0.9085]. The negative controls matched the baseline exactly at 0.9049 [0.9013, 0.9085].

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.002549 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], paired randomisation p=0.106, Cohen's dz=0.25). There is no statistically significant difference because the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9087 [0.9057, 0.9116], while the baseline achieved 0.9061 [0.9022, 0.9099]. The negative controls matched the baseline exactly at 0.9061 [0.9022, 0.9099].

The confidence intervals in both cohorts exclude gains of the target magnitude (0.0125098 proportion) under the stated uncertainty model, as the upper bounds (0.0031 and 0.0055) lie below the margin. This preserves the registered label of inconclusive while explaining that the data excludes the worthwhile gain. The training curves in Figure 3 and Figure 5 show overlapping trajectories, consistent with the null contrast.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that spectral entropy minimization of input projection weights did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The measured outcome licenses a conclusion that, for someone choosing between these methods in this regime, the intervention offers no reliable accuracy advantage over standard weight decay. This does not establish that the mechanism is inactive, only that the accuracy contrast does not detect it.

A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that the spectral entropy penalty is too weak to alter the optimization trajectory meaningfully relative to the classification loss. An alternative is that the input projection layer's spectral geometry is not a bottleneck for subject-disjoint generalization in this task. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is stable across seeds, as the effect size remained small and nonsignificant in both cohorts. However, the confirmatory cohort is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, so generalization beyond this split remains untested.

The finding stands against specific cited papers in nuanced ways. Entropy maximization of weight noise was refuted in a similar setting [1], and our result suggests entropy minimization also fails to boost accuracy, implying entropy manipulation of weights may not be the critical factor for robustness here. This contrasts with work suggesting low-entropy latent variables hurt OOD performance [4], indicating that entropy effects may differ between activations and weights. Time series OOD challenges persist despite regularization [6], and our result adds that spectral entropy minimization does not resolve them in this architecture. Regularization shortcomings in non-iid settings [8] may explain why a spectral penalty alone cannot overcome distribution shift without stronger inductive biases.

What would settle the question next is a direct measurement of the weight spectra during training to confirm whether the operator successfully minimized entropy without degrading task loss. Additionally, testing on a dataset with stronger distribution shifts would determine if the effect is task-dependent. A null outcome owes the reader these mechanistic checks, and we do not rewrite the inconclusive accuracy result as a positive finding.

=== limitations ===
A key limitation is that both negative controls were inert as implemented: bit-identical to the baseline on every seed in both cohorts. This means they carry no diagnostic information and cannot validate the harness or the implementation. We state this clearly to prevent misinterpretation of the control contrasts. The registered primary contrast is unaffected by this inertness but stays inconclusive.

Another limitation is the power qualification. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

Finally, evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects, but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. We do not call this out-of-distribution or domain generalisation beyond the subject split. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that spectral entropy minimization of input projection weights did not significantly improve held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series transformer. The measured outcome licenses a decision that practitioners should not expect accuracy gains from this specific regularization in this regime. The inconclusive result in both primary and replication cohorts suggests the effect, if any, is smaller than the registered worthwhile margin. Future work should measure weight spectra directly to confirm operator activity and test on datasets with stronger distribution shifts to settle whether spectral geometry influences robustness in more challenging settings.

Conversely, if spectral entropy minimization yields no benefit, resources should focus on alternative architectural or optimization strategies. This paper reports a preregistered experiment testing whether spectral entropy minimization of input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay.

We address the open problem of what specific weight geometry facilitates feature learning versus kernel regime behavior in finite-width networks. Our study isolates the effect of spectral entropy regularization on the input projection layer of a transformer encoder, holding all other architectural and optimization factors constant. We evaluate performance on held-out subjects to ensure claims about generalization reflect subject-disjoint robustness rather than random split variance.

The contributions of this work are:
- We execute a preregistered test of spectral entropy minimization on input projections in a time-series transformer, reporting both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts.
- We provide exact quantitative estimates of the effect size with 95% confidence intervals, determining whether the effect exceeds a registered worthwhile margin.
- We document the inertness of registered negative controls, clarifying their inability to validate the experimental harness.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report results honestly against this prediction, labeling any unforeseen finding as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research on generalization in sequential and structured data highlights significant challenges regarding distribution shifts and model capacity. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [6]. This motivates the use of subject-disjoint evaluation splits to assess robustness to unseen populations rather than random data partitions. When training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting and regularization strategies may fail to discriminate classes from different tasks [8]. This underscores the need for regularization techniques that explicitly account for the geometry of learned representations in non-iid settings.

Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness. Entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters was investigated to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift, but results refuted the hypothesis that it improves out-of-distribution accuracy in attention-based architectures [1]. This suggests that explicit entropy maximization may actively impair performance in this regime. Conversely, studies on latent variables indicate that low-entropy intermediate representations can hurt out-of-distribution performance, as removing low-entropy bits may benefit robustness [4]. This presents a tension: while low-entropy latents may harm OOD performance, we test whether low-entropy *weights* facilitate feature selection. The relationship between entropy and robustness thus depends on whether entropy is measured in activations or parameters, and whether it is maximized or minimized.

Regularization theory notes that empirical risk minimization is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning [5]. Regularization principles, such as structural risk minimization, are required to characterize optimal learning in multiclass settings. This supports the investigation of spectral regularization as a means to steer optimization towards flatter or more structured minima. However, the specific impact of singular value entropy on the input projection layer remains untested in transformer-based time-series models.

Methods involving projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality and regularization, though often in linear programming contexts. While data-driven projections can accelerate solving linear programs and improve solution quality [2], their extension to neural network weight spectra requires empirical validation. The gap this work addresses is that while prior work examines entropy maximization for weight noise robustness and singular value decay in Bayesian networks, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We position this study against the themes of spectral geometry and entropy-based regularization, testing whether minimizing spectral entropy in input weights aligns with the feature-learning hypothesis in a subject-disjoint setting.

=== method ===
The method centers on the Spectral Entropy Minimization operator applied to the input projection weights. The hypothesis posits that enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum enhances feature learning by encouraging the model to select dominant temporal modes rather than distributing energy uniformly. This operator is the registered intervention, and its comparator holds all other training dynamics fixed.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. Its term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The scope is the singular value distribution of the weight matrix. Specifically, the operator retrieves the target parameter tensor W (shape [64, 9]), computes singular values sigma via SVD, and normalizes them to probabilities p by dividing by their sum plus an epsilon safeguard. It then computes entropy H as the negative sum of p times log(p). The loss term is scaled by a coefficient of 0.01 and returned to the harness for addition to the objective. This formulation ensures H is non-negative and minimized when one singular value dominates.

The registered comparator is the baseline condition, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective.

The registered negative controls were intended to isolate specific implementation artifacts. The first negative control computes spectral entropy on W detached from the graph, preventing gradient flow. This was intended to test whether the gradient signal from the entropy term, rather than the term's value, drives any observed effect. However, as noted in the Limitations, both negative controls were inert as implemented. The method focuses on the operator's mathematical expression of the hypothesis: that minimizing spectral entropy on input projections shapes the weight geometry to favor dominant temporal modes. We do not claim attention stability or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone; the measured outcome is held-out classification accuracy.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design prioritizes subject-disjoint generalization over random-split performance. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of robustness to unseen individuals, which a random split would not, as random splits allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing. This design choice ensures that claims about generalization reflect performance on new subjects, not merely interpolation within a subject's data distribution. Variation is attributed to seeds, not subjects, as the experimental unit is the seeded training run.

Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance by ensuring both arms see the same data ordering and initialization. This allows for paired statistical tests that are more sensitive to small effects than unpaired tests. The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication in the sense of new subjects or datasets; it is a replication on new seeds within the same subject-disjoint split. This distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects or architectures.

The negative controls' intended alternative explanation was to verify that any observed effect stemmed from the gradient signal of the entropy term rather than computational artifacts. The first negative control detached the weight tensor from the graph. However, the observed contrast supports no diagnostic conclusion because both negative controls were inert as implemented: bit-identical to the baseline on every seed in both cohorts. This inertness means they carry no diagnostic information and cannot validate the harness or the implementation. The registered primary contrast is unaffected by this inertness but remains inconclusive based on the measured outcomes. The analysis uses bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds to quantify uncertainty, preserving registered labels without equating nonsignificance with equality.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, stating each preregistered decision. We never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. Figure 1 illustrates the flow from UCI HAR data through the PreNormTransformerEncoder, applying SpectralEntropyRegularization to input_proj.weight at the loss term across registered arms. Figure 2 and Figure 4 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. Figure 3 and Figure 5 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

In the primary cohort, across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0004419 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], paired randomisation p=0.75, Cohen's dz=0.05). There is no statistically significant difference because the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9053 [0.9023, 0.9085], while the baseline achieved 0.9049 [0.9013, 0.9085]. The negative controls matched the baseline exactly at 0.9049 [0.9013, 0.9085].

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.002549 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], paired randomisation p=0.106, Cohen's dz=0.25). There is no statistically significant difference because the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9087 [0.9057, 0.9116], while the baseline achieved 0.9061 [0.9022, 0.9099]. The negative controls matched the baseline exactly at 0.9061 [0.9022, 0.9099].

The confidence intervals in both cohorts exclude gains of the target magnitude (0.0125098 proportion) under the stated uncertainty model, as the upper bounds (0.0031 and 0.0055) lie below the margin. This preserves the registered label of inconclusive while explaining that the data excludes the worthwhile gain. The training curves in Figure 3 and Figure 5 show overlapping trajectories, consistent with the null contrast.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that spectral entropy minimization of input projection weights did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The measured outcome licenses a conclusion that, for someone choosing between these methods in this regime, the intervention offers no reliable accuracy advantage over standard weight decay. This does not establish that the mechanism is inactive, only that the accuracy contrast does not detect it.

A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that the spectral entropy penalty is too weak to alter the optimization trajectory meaningfully relative to the classification loss. An alternative is that the input projection layer's spectral geometry is not a bottleneck for subject-disjoint generalization in this task. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is stable across seeds, as the effect size remained small and nonsignificant in both cohorts. However, the confirmatory cohort is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, so generalization beyond this split remains untested.

The finding stands against specific cited papers in nuanced ways. Entropy maximization of weight noise was refuted in a similar setting [1], and our result suggests entropy minimization also fails to boost accuracy, implying entropy manipulation of weights may not be the critical factor for robustness here. This contrasts with work suggesting low-entropy latent variables hurt OOD performance [4], indicating that entropy effects may differ between activations and weights. Time series OOD challenges persist despite regularization [6], and our result adds that spectral entropy minimization does not resolve them in this architecture. Regularization shortcomings in non-iid settings [8] may explain why a spectral penalty alone cannot overcome distribution shift without stronger inductive biases.

What would settle the question next is a direct measurement of the weight spectra during training to confirm whether the operator successfully minimized entropy without degrading task loss. Additionally, testing on a dataset with stronger distribution shifts would determine if the effect is task-dependent. A null outcome owes the reader these mechanistic checks, and we do not rewrite the inconclusive accuracy result as a positive finding.

=== limitations ===
A key limitation is that both negative controls were inert as implemented: bit-identical to the baseline on every seed in both cohorts. This means they carry no diagnostic information and cannot validate the harness or the implementation. We state this clearly to prevent misinterpretation of the control contrasts. The registered primary contrast is unaffected by this inertness but stays inconclusive.

Another limitation is the power qualification. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

Finally, evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects, but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. We do not call this out-of-distribution or domain generalisation beyond the subject split. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that spectral entropy minimization of input projection weights did not significantly improve held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series transformer. The measured outcome licenses a decision that practitioners should not expect accuracy gains from this specific regularization in this regime. The inconclusive result in both primary and replication cohorts suggests the effect, if any, is smaller than the registered worthwhile margin. Future work should measure weight spectra directly to confirm operator activity and test on datasets with stronger distribution shifts to settle whether spectral geometry influences robustness in more challenging settings.

[5] Julian Asilis, Siddartha Devic et al. Regularization and Optimal Multiclass Learning (2024).
[6] Xin Wu, Fei Teng et al. Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey (2025).
[8] Timothée Lesort, Andrei Stoian et al. Regularization Shortcomings for Continual Learning (2019).

+Two negative controls were declared.
+The first computes the spectral entropy of the input projection weights detached from the computation graph, so that no gradient flows from it; the second is standard weight decay with no spectral entropy term.
+They were intended to separate the effect of the spectral entropy gradient from the effect of computing the term and from generic regularization.
+As implemented, neither control changed training: the first computed a value that never entered the training objective, and the second applied only the weight decay that the optimizer already applies in every condition.
+The harness recorded zero intervention activations for both controls on every seed, and their held-out accuracies are identical to the baseline's on all 43 seeds of both cohorts.
